papers.abstract: Attention costs $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ in the number of tokens. Vector-quantized attention reduces this to $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ by clustering the $N$ keys, attending to the $M$ codewords instead, and its adaptive form, AVQ-attention, concentrates codebook resolution where a query's attention mass actually falls. We present AVQ-Attention-2, a better design that merges it with exact local attention and attends to the mean of each cluster's keys rather than to a codeword. We show three improvements: consistently better quality at comparable cost; training that now also costs $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$; and an approximation accurate enough that the layer can be dropped into a pretrained transformer without fine-tuning. Across a variety of sequence lengths the result is competitive not merely with other approximate attention but with exact dense attention, running faster than FlashAttention at little to no loss in quality.
authors: Winfried van den Dool, Patrick Forr\'e, Amir Habibian, Yuki M. Asano, Max Welling
bullets: Reduces attention complexity from quadratic to O(NM) by clustering keys and attending to cluster representatives.
Uses adaptive quantization to allocate codebook resolution where each query’s attention mass is concentrated.
Adds exact local attention and represents clusters by the mean of their keys rather than codewords.
Achieves better quality at comparable cost and is accurate enough to replace attention in pretrained transformers without fine-tuning.
Across sequence lengths, competes with exact dense attention and runs faster than FlashAttention with little to no quality loss.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive vector-quantized attention with linear-cost training and drop-in approximation for pretrained transformers.
papers.title: AVQ-Attention-2: Adaptive Vector-Quantized Attention with Exact Local Blocks and Linear-Cost Training
papers.tldr: AVQ-Attention-2 combines adaptive vector-quantized attention with exact local attention to achieve linear-cost training and inference while retaining quality competitive with dense attention.

papers.abstract: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.
bullets: The study examines why linear attention underperforms softmax attention on associative recall in language modeling.
Synthetic experiments find that recall capacity scales with state size similarly across tested linear-attention architectures.
Even a single sufficiently scaled layer can retrieve thousands of long-distance associations.
In-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting improve recall benchmarks and narrow the gap to softmax attention.
These gains come without architectural or compute-budget changes, but with a slight cost to general language modeling.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates linear attention recall capacity and training interventions, directly relevant to efficient attention and language modeling.
papers.title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
papers.tldr: Linear-attention models can recall far more associations than standard training elicits, and targeted recall-focused supervision substantially improves their long-distance retrieval.

papers.abstract: Self-attention's quadratic complexity constitutes a core bottleneck for Vision Transformers (ViTs). Existing efficiency-oriented optimizations, including softmax-based and linear attention (LA) variants, generally compromise model representational capacity, leading to inevitable performance degradation. We propose a novel linear attention which alleviates this efficiency-capability dilemma. For the first time, we embed an Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification (ACCAP) mechanism into the QKV projection of linear attention, which enables the model to retain high-dimensional feature information while performing computations with reduced channels. We further fuse a focused kernel function and a self-gating module into ACCAP to construct a lightweight linear attention module (ACCAP-LA). Our theoretical analysis shows that, compared to standard linear attention, ACCAP-LA reduces the attention module's parameter count by 79.17% and FLOPs by 77.5%. Extensive experiments demonstrate ACCAP-LA's effectiveness: when applied to ViT, it achieves 79.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with only 5.8M parameters, and more notably, it boasts strong cross-architecture compatibility, boosting EfficientViT-b1 and PVT-T by 3.3% and 3.4% respectively.
authors: Senqi Guan, Xianchao Zhang, Moyan Tian, Linlin Zong, Wenxin Liang, Xinyue Liu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–capability trade-off caused by quadratic self-attention and capacity loss in efficient attention variants.
Embeds Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification into QKV projections, with a focused kernel and self-gating module.
Reduces linear-attention parameter count by 79.17% and FLOPs by 77.5% relative to standard linear attention.
Achieves 79.4% ImageNet-1K Top-1 accuracy with 5.8M parameters in ViT.
Improves EfficientViT-b1 and PVT-T accuracy by 3.3% and 3.4%, respectively, indicating cross-architecture compatibility.

papers.title: Simultaneously Boosting Efficiency and Capability for Linear Attention via Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification
papers.tldr: ACCAP-LA makes linear attention substantially more efficient while preserving or improving ViT representation capability through adaptive channel compression and activation purification.

papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
bullets: Quantising the transformer-based Depth Anything V2 directly causes severe information loss because many attention weights fall below int8 precision.
The proposed ResNet-34 U-Net student, distilled from Depth Anything V2-Large, runs at 27.1 FPS using 24.5M parameters.
Its int8 predictions closely match its float version (Pearson 0.99993) and achieve the best held-out simulated-yard accuracy among tested onboard models (AbsRel 0.269).
On 1,000 stereo-verified real-drive points, it performs comparably to the vendor’s Depth Anything V2-Small while running faster (27.1 vs. 21.6 FPS).
Integrated with mapping, planning, and SLAM, the system reaches goals without contact in most hardware-in-the-loop yard trials, though less often than with exact obstacle maps.

papers.selection_reason: Attention-free depth distillation enabling onboard robot navigation on low-power hardware; efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: An attention-free, distilled depth model enables real-time monocular obstacle ranging and navigation on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo-8L hardware.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a serious competitor to gradient-boosted trees, predicting on a new table in a single forward pass by in-context learning. However, their attention is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which caps pretraining at small synthetic tables and forces inference on large ones to rely on chunking or subsampling. Row-compression models reduce the feature-wise cost, but only by discarding the cell-level representation, and remain quadratic in the number of samples. We introduce InducedTFM, which replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the Set Transformer, preserving cell-level representations while making its cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation, InducedTFM matches its accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, and clearly outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost. It overtakes TabICLv2 in inference time on narrow tables, reaching a 30x speed-up at 640K rows, although row compression remains preferable on wide tables.
authors: Salome Gobbi, Nicolas Atienza, Nicola Cancedda, Michael Arbel
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost that limits TFM pretraining and inference on large tables.
Replaces both attention stages in a bidimensional TFM with Set Transformer-style induced attention.
Preserves cell-level representations while achieving linear cost in the number of samples and features.

papers.selection_reason: Induced attention makes tabular foundation models sub-quadratic, directly fitting efficient-attention research.
papers.title: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
papers.tldr: InducedTFM uses induced attention to make tabular foundation models linear in both rows and features while preserving cell-level representations, matching full attention accuracy and greatly accelerating inference on narrow, large tables.

papers.abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.
authors: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
bullets: Addresses the slowdown, accuracy loss, and context-window limits of one-pass long-context inference.
Uses training-free block-sparse attention to read local and strided spans from a single KV cache in one batched forward pass.
Employs a stair position schedule to keep spans within the model’s trained position range.
Matches grid probing’s accuracy and reach across long video, long-text inference, and image grounding while using a fraction of its cost.
Reports up to roughly 10-point gains over single-pass inference, finds information beyond the context window, and can be as fast as one-tenth of grid probing.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free block-sparse attention for native grid probing over long contexts; fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
papers.tldr: Factorized Context Attention natively reproduces grid probing’s long-context benefits with much lower inference cost in frozen language and vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often retain only a limited set of past token positions for an attention query. A common strategy scores positions individually and keeps the highest-ranked K. Yet attention weights are renormalized over the chosen set: two individually important positions need not form the best pair. We ask whether independent ranking suffices even when each importance score measures the exact downstream change in next-token predictions caused by deleting that position alone. It does not. A four-position construction makes the ranked pair incur 133.2 times the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of the optimal pair, and a parametric family proves that this multiplicative gap is unbounded. An exact exchange identity and preference reversals for every K >= 2 explain the interaction. In exhaustive frozen-model audits of SmolLM2, Gemma, and Qwen, exact-singleton Top-4 leaves at least 10% relative improvement within a fully enumerated 24-position candidate pool in 55/60, 49/60, and 60/60 cases, respectively. SwapCert, a same-budget one-swap audit, detects 157/164 such cases and returns directly checkable improving supports. A KL-margin certificate relates support fidelity to next-token stability; larger-budget, multi-layer cached-decoding experiments measure predictive fidelity at K = 128 and 256. These results establish joint support quality as an essential object of analysis for sparse attention and motivate downstream-aware support selection under inference constraints.
bullets: Individually important positions may form a poor set after attention renormalization; optimal selection must account for interactions.
A four-position example yields a 133.2× KL-divergence gap, while a parametric family shows the gap can be unbounded.
Exhaustive audits find at least 10% improvement opportunities over exact-singleton Top-4 in 55/60 SmolLM2, 49/60 Gemma, and 60/60 Qwen cases.
SwapCert detects 157/164 such cases using a same-budget one-swap audit and provides checkable improving supports.
KL-margin certificates and larger-budget experiments connect support quality to next-token stability and predictive fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes top-K token selection and joint support quality in sparse LLM attention, directly relevant to token pruning and efficient attention.
papers.title: When Exact Token Importance Is Not Enough: Limits of Top-K Selection in LLM Attention
papers.tldr: Independent Top-K token selection can fail badly in sparse LLM attention—even with exact single-token importance—because token interactions make joint support quality essential.

papers.abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
authors: Junsoo Oh, Jihun Yun, Junhyuck Kim, Hanbaek Lyu
bullets: Linear attention avoids growing key-value caches but can lose information through fixed-size memory collisions.
The method uses a delta state for current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of past delta states.
An adaptive readout combines both states to retrieve information across multiple timescales.
A chunkwise parallel formulation supports hardware-efficient training.
Experiments report improved performance across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation, alongside evaluations of efficiency and memory use.

papers.abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.
authors: Xi Lin, Chengruidong Zhang, Huiqiang Jiang, Xiao Li, Zekun Wang, Junda Feng, Yunfei Mao, Siqi Zhang, Siyu Wang, Man Yuan, Rui Men, Bo Zheng, Dayiheng Liu, Bohan Zhuang, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited parallelism from GDN’s sequential chunk dependencies, especially for long contexts and small batch sizes.
Uses decay-aware boundary preparation and Dual CP to share summary computation across parallelism levels.
Adds workload-adaptive Auto CP and context-parallel-aware kernel co-design for improved efficiency.
Reports 1.7×–3.1× forward and up to 4.4× backward speedup over FLA on one GPU.
Across eight GPUs and up to 1M-token contexts, Dual CP reaches up to 4.8× forward speedup and 4.4× combined forward/backward speedup over FLA KCP.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over tens of thousands of tokens dominates the generation time of video diffusion transformers, because its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. The FP4 matrix products of modern GPUs can speed up attention, but the 4-bit rounding of the queries Q and the keys K introduces large errors. We show that the exponential in softmax amplifies the error of their product QK, which therefore dominates the attention error. We propose DeCo-Attention, a co-design of algorithm and system for low-precision attention. DeCo-Attention is training-free and compensates the rounding error of Q and K along a few principal directions found by a per-head eigendecomposition. The lightweight compensation terms are appended to Q and K as extra channels, so the FP4 matrix product corrects its own rounding error while it computes the attention scores. Once the products run in FP4, the softmax bounds the kernel, and we optimize the softmax so that the gain of FP4 computation translates into realized speedup. With QK in FP4, we implement DeCo-Attention with the rest of attention in FP8 on GB300 and VR200 and in FP4 on RTX PRO 6000. On Wan2.2, these kernels run 2.13x, 2.49x, and 2.82x faster than BF16 attention, and the whole generation runs 1.55x, 1.68x, and 1.80x faster. On four video generation models, the FP8 configuration achieves LPIPS comparable to prior 8-bit QK methods, and the fully FP4 configuration lower LPIPS than prior fully 4-bit kernels.
authors: Yuhang He, Harrison Zhang, Fanrong Li, Chang Liu, RuQing G. Xu, Perkz Zheng, Zhenhua Wang, Rajeev Rao, Mengdi Wang, Sharan Chetlur, Jun Yang
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.
Uses per-head eigendecomposition to identify principal error directions in quantized queries and keys.
Appends compensation channels to Q and K, allowing the FP4 matrix product to correct its own rounding error.
Combines FP4 QK with optimized softmax and lower-precision attention components for practical speedups.
Reports 2.13–2.82× faster attention and 1.55–1.80× faster generation on Wan2.2, with competitive or improved LPIPS versus prior low-precision methods.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DeCo-Attention, a training-free method to compensate for low-precision (FP4) errors in video diffusion transformers. This directly addresses efficient attention mechanisms in video generation models.
papers.title: DeCo-Attention: Decompose to Compensate for Low-Precision Attention
papers.tldr: DeCo-Attention makes long-context video diffusion attention faster in FP4 by correcting QK rounding errors with lightweight, training-free compensation.

papers.abstract: Recently, physics-inspired neural networks have gained widespread attention due to their interpretability. The closed-form, frequency-time decoupled solution of the wave equation offers linear complexity and allows different frequency components to evolve independently, making it a potential alternative solution for efficient image super-resolution. Therefore, a physics-inspired wave evolution attention framework is proposed, namely WaveSR. The WaveSR framework involves two key modules, i.e., wave evolution attention (WEA) and Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network (FA-FFN). The WEA module achieves feature interactions through the analytical solution of the 2D wave equation in the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) domain, enabling independent evolution of different frequency components with learnable wave speed \(c\) and damping coefficient \(\alpha\). The FA-FFN module realizes adaptive frequency feature selection through learnable spectral modulation, effectively enhancing feature representation capability. Subsequently, we employ a two-stage training strategy with a hybrid objective that combines a spatial-domain pixel loss and a frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality. Our method provides a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient image super-resolution.
authors: Xiaoyan Lei, Biao Luo, Wenlong Zhang, Tingwen Huang, Chunhua Yang, Weihua Gui
bullets: Targets efficient image super-resolution using the closed-form, frequency–time-decoupled wave equation.
Wave Evolution Attention performs FFT-domain feature interactions with independently evolving frequency components.
Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network selects and enhances frequency features through learnable spectral modulation.
A two-stage training strategy combines spatial pixel loss with frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality.
The work is presented as a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient super-resolution.

papers.abstract: Converting pretrained softmax Transformers to efficient attention often causes substantial performance degradation, while recovery typically requires costly fine-tuning. We propose ET (Efficient Transfer), a framework for high-fidelity attention conversion with minimal optimization cost. ET combines exact local and shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating, achieving linear complexity in sequence length. To preserve pretrained knowledge, ET freezes pretrained weights and calibrates only newly introduced parameters through alternating least squares on a small set of unlabeled samples, without gradient updates. On ImageNet-1K, ET achieves 79.64% and 81.55% top-1 accuracy on DeiT-S and DeiT-B, respectively, within 0.25 percentage points of their softmax teachers. At $768\times768$, ET outperforms T$^5$ by 3.59 percentage points at comparable inference FLOPs, without gradient-based fine-tuning. On DiT-XL/2, ET achieves an FID-50K of 2.59 with only 250 LoRA updates. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, ET matches the teacher's GenEval score at 1K resolution with just 0.73 A100 GPU-hours of gradient-free conversion and a 1.39$\times$ inference speedup.
authors: Guangfu Guo, Xiaoqian Lu, Linsey Pang, Weiran Yao, Haolin Chen, Long Cheng, Kunpeng Liu
bullets: Addresses the performance loss and costly fine-tuning typically associated with efficient-attention conversion.
Combines exact local/shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating.

On ImageNet-1K, remains within 0.25 percentage points of DeiT-S and DeiT-B softmax teachers; also improves over T$^5$ at comparable FLOPs.
Demonstrates gradient-free conversion for diffusion models, matching Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium's GenEval score with faster inference.

papers.abstract: ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD) is a sample-efficient objective for pre-training text encoders, and RTD-trained models such as DeBERTaV3 are strong on classification benchmarks. The same models, however, are known to be poor backbones for embedding tasks such as retrieval and semantic similarity: the binary "original vs. replaced" signal does not ask the final layer to retain the token identity and contextual content that dense representations rely on. We introduce ModernELECTRA, a pre-training recipe that keeps RTD as the main objective and adds a lightweight auxiliary task, boundary-window reconstruction. For every token, we sample a window of 3-12 tokens that strictly contains it and reconstruct the token's original identity only from the discriminator's hidden states at the two window boundaries. The task costs one small FFN at training time and is discarded afterwards, yet it forces every final-layer state to carry information about its neighbourhood. Combined with a frozen, separately pre-trained generator, a temperature curriculum for hard negatives and a 512-to-8192 length curriculum, we train two compact encoders: EdgeCoder-31M, an 8-layer English model, and EdgeCoder-Multilingual-61M, a 16-layer model covering 46 languages, each on about 1T tokens. They reach 86.0 and 85.1 on GLUE. The English model outperforms Ettin-Enc-32m (83.5) and MiniLM-L12 (84.6) on GLUE while matching them on MTEB English v2 (51.1), and the multilingual model outperforms the 2.3x larger mmBERT-small on GLUE and Multilingual MiniLM and mDistilBERT on XTREME over the languages it covers. We also describe FlashDeBERTa, our open-source fused implementation of DeBERTa's disentangled attention that stores no $n \times n$ score matrix: at 4096 tokens it is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory than the reference implementation, and it loads existing DeBERTa checkpoints unchanged.
authors: Mykhailo Shtopko, Ihor Stepanov, Dmytro Vodianytskyi, Oleksandr Lukashov
bullets: RTD is efficient for classification but often yields weak dense embeddings because it does not preserve token identity and contextual content.
The auxiliary task reconstructs each token from hidden states at the boundaries of a surrounding 3–12-token window, using a small training-only FFN.
Two compact models trained on about 1T tokens achieve GLUE scores of 86.0 (31M English) and 85.1 (61M multilingual, 46 languages).

The English model matches comparable models on MTEB English v2 while outperforming them on GLUE; the multilingual model improves over larger or established multilingual baselines on reported benchmarks.
FlashDeBERTa provides a memory-efficient fused DeBERTa attention implementation, but its reported speed and memory gains are specific to the reference comparison.

papers.title: ModernELECTRA: Replaced-Token Detection with Boundary-Window Reconstruction for Compact Encoders that Classify and Embed
papers.tldr: ModernELECTRA adds boundary-window reconstruction to RTD pre-training, producing compact encoders that retain strong classification and embedding performance.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.
bullets: Source tokens act as local spatial anchors, enabling viewpoint-dependent token culling without explicit 3D geometry.
A lightweight router ranks tokens using source features and the target viewpoint; the decoder attends only to a fixed top-token budget.
Router training uses decoder attention supervision and non-maximum suppression to reduce redundant selections.
With 24 source images, rendering is 6.4× faster than LagerNVS while achieving PSNR only 0.68 dB lower.
A single token ranking supports changing the compute budget at render time.

papers.abstract: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
authors: Da Xiao, Qingye Meng, Shengping Li, Xingyuan Yuan
bullets: Motivation: Standard Transformer circuits have relatively fixed information pathways across heads and layers.
Method: Loom attention interleaves vertical attention over earlier head outputs with horizontal token attention, using normalized, gated linear attention over per-token matrix memories.
Architecture: LoomFormer uses dual residual streams, separating control in vector states from content in matrix states.
Results: Across language modeling and downstream tasks, it matches models trained with over 3× compute and recent residual-stream baselines trained with roughly 1.7–2.8× compute.
Scope: Demonstrated across multiple model sizes and training-token budgets; code is publicly available. ],

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.
authors: YuanShuo Wang, Jianchao Tan, Lei Gong, Teng Wang, Wenqi Lou, Xuehai Zhou
bullets: Addresses retrieval overhead and the limits of uniform page scoring in sparse attention.
Uses a Lightweight Gate Estimator during prefill to skip low-value regions with under 1% added dense-prefill time.
Extracts compact, calibration-free features for both page- and token-level scoring.
A distance-aware two-level selector ranks near and far pages and candidate tokens under a shared budget.
On Qwen3-8B at 512K context, achieves up to 5.49× operator and 2.97× whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse region-aware attention for long-context LLM decoding with lightweight page/token selection and retrieval.
papers.title: Near-Far Attention: Region-Aware Sparse Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Near-Far Attention accelerates long-context LLM decoding by sparsely retrieving tokens with region-aware scoring while preserving task quality comparable to full attention.

papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.
authors: Marco Pichler, Patrick Podest, G\"unter Klambauer, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Edge forecasting requires fast refreshes, bounded latency and memory, and stable accuracy as observations accumulate.
Causal recurrent models support fixed-size state updates, unlike non-causal models and KV-cache approaches whose costs grow with history.
The authors persist recurrent states across refreshes and verify equivalence with full recomputation.
Nine TSFM configurations are evaluated on univariate forecasting across a GPU and three edge devices.
Most models lose accuracy beyond their trained context; only TiRex-2 meets all requirements, including constant resource use over one million steps.

papers.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
authors: Fu Dai, Haodi Quan, Kamal Taha
bullets: Short-sequence failures are mainly attributed to rotary positional encoding rather than content matching.
Random gaps in position IDs let the indexer and frozen teacher learn long-range positions without processing long sequences.
An 8K-distilled indexer nearly matches 32K- and, on one model, 64K-distilled quality; the reported training-cost reduction is about 6× per token.
3–4-bit key quantization requires no retraining; 4-bit keys change perplexity by at most 0.05 and yield 1.6–2.2× faster scans.
Benefits vary by model and serving setting: position compression can be competitive, and decoding speedups appear mainly for long contexts with multiple streams.

papers.selection_reason: Improves sparse-attention indexer distillation for long-context serving with position-skipped training and quantization, relevant to efficient long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
papers.tldr: Position-skipped distillation trains sparse-attention indexers on short sequences that generalize to long contexts, substantially reducing training cost while preserving quality in several models.

papers.abstract: High-resolution images contain rich visual details that require fine geometric structures for faithful 3D reconstruction. However, generating extremely detailed 3D geometry from images requires substantial computational resources and training data, making high-resolution geometry generation challenging for existing state-of-the-art models. In this paper, we present SuperFine3D, an efficient framework for generating extremely detailed 3D geometry through global-local recursive refinement. SuperFine3D learns a shared refinement operator from paired coarse-to-fine representations and recursively reuses it to progressively synthesize finer geometry beyond the training resolutions, without requiring additional paired supervision at target resolutions. To make recursive refinement computationally efficient, we introduce spatial-cell attention, which restricts high-resolution interactions to local spatial neighborhoods while maintaining bounded communication across neighboring cells. We further propose spatially anchored cross-scale guidance, which leverages globally contextualized coarse geometry to guide local detail synthesis and preserve structural consistency. In addition, geometry-aware training objectives encourage the refinement process to preserve stable geometric structures while introducing fine-grained surface details. Experiments demonstrate that SuperFine3D generates geometry at a $4096^3$ decoder-grid resolution, corresponding to a sparse $256^3$ latent lattice, using a shared refinement operator trained only on $512^3$--$1024^3$ representations. Compared with a full-attention recursive baseline, SuperFine3D achieves a $9.4\times$ speedup in end-to-end inference and reduces peak GPU memory usage by $23.0\%$, while improving cross-scale structural consistency and producing cleaner surfaces with finer geometric details.
authors: Lihan Li, Junwei Zhou, Yu-wing Tai
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and data demands of high-resolution 3D geometry generation.
Learns a shared coarse-to-fine refinement operator and reuses it recursively beyond the training resolutions.
Uses spatial-cell attention for efficient local interactions and spatially anchored cross-scale guidance for global structural consistency.
Trained on 512³–1024³ representations, it generates geometry at 4096³ decoder-grid resolution with a sparse 256³ latent lattice.
Compared with full-attention recursive refinement, it achieves 9.4× faster inference, 23.0% lower peak GPU memory, and cleaner, finer surfaces.

papers.title: SuperFine3D: Efficient Global-Local Recursive Refinement for Extremely Detailed 3D Geometry Generation
papers.tldr: SuperFine3D efficiently generates extremely detailed 3D geometry by recursively refining coarse structures with localized attention and global guidance.

papers.abstract: The domain of genomic language models (gLMs) has advanced rapidly, with models pretrained on diverse multi-species genomic corpora demonstrating their remarkable capabilities. While the effect of simple nucleotide-level tokenization on long-context modeling is well established, overlapping k-mer tokenization remains underexplored in causal pretraining, despite its rich neighborhood information. Here, we thoroughly revisit overlapping tokenization and introduce HGDNA, a hybrid linear-attention gLM with causal language modeling (CLM) pretraining and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation, using a species-classification auxiliary task and shared class tokens. HGDNA delivers competitive performance across sequence classification and frozen-embedding evaluations, supporting both short-range and long-range tasks with 30M parameters and 19B pretraining tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/HGDNA
authors: Xudong Wang, Siwei Cheng, Haozhe Hu
bullets: Addresses the limited study of overlapping k-mers for causal genomic pretraining, motivated by their richer neighborhood information.
Uses a hybrid linear-attention architecture pretrained with causal language modeling and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation.
Adds a species-classification auxiliary task with shared class tokens.
Achieves competitive results on sequence-classification and frozen-embedding evaluations spanning short- and long-range tasks.
The abstract reports a 30M-parameter model trained on 19B genomic tokens; broader generalization beyond the evaluated tasks is not specified.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Zihao Yang, Quanjiang Li, Haijiang Li, Jiancheng Pan, Qichao Zhao, Zihan Dong, Qiushi Shi, Jinshi Liu
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of dense attention during long-sequence prefill and the limitations of uniform head-level sparsity.
Uses shared cross-head importance estimation, then applies query-specific decisions for computational budgets and token selection.

Boundary Voting refines tokens near the selection cutoff using actual query–key scores without changing the initial selection size.
Length-specialized kernels reduce the overhead of executing dynamic sparse patterns; experiments report better benchmark scores and faster prefill attention than prior sparse-attention baselines.

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.
authors: Zhiling Zhou, Jiachun Pan, Fengzhuo Zhang, Dirk Bergemann, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: CFG’s conditional and unconditional logits both strongly encode previous-token repetition; their difference primarily captures texture information.
Greedy decoding from conditional logits alone can yield nearly pure-color images because repetition semantics obscure texture.
Theoretical and empirical analyses attribute this shared repetition bias to image texture sparsity, not pretraining failure.
CFG improves quality by rectifying the repetition bias during inference.
Attention Weight Reuse cuts about 25% of attention computation with little performance degradation across models.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Overview of the proof. (1) Training WV makes text and background tokens favor background repetition, while feature tokens favor feature repetition. papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.
authors: Nurlan Nazaraliyev, Elaheh Sadredini, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
bullets: Top-$p$ selection adapts computation to attention distributions, avoiding top-$k$’s fixed-budget waste or context loss.
Integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM with scheduler-decoupled block selection and a two-stream pipeline that overlaps selection with layer computation.
Uses a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel to reduce selection cost.
Relocates tokens based on prefill attention scores to reduce intra-block sparsity and inflated selection budgets.
Reports 1.17×–1.80× faster sparsity analysis, negligible accuracy loss, and up to 8× larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
bullets: Targets serialization cost, repeated schema prefill, and decoding that is unaware of live catalogs and MVCC.
Uses an in-process Rust runtime with Python, Rust, and OpenCypher models ranging from 16.8M to 1.07B parameters.
Introduces epoch-invalidated schema KV caching, catalog/source-span logit masking, and an MVCC gate for read-only queries.
Reports 4.91–13.68× faster warm CPU time-to-first-token, 0.0% hallucination leak, and 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool-planning tasks.
Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation recovers 13.61 MBPP points while operating without VRAM for the distillation verifier.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.
authors: Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, Yiming Gan, Jingwen Leng, Minyi Guo, Yu Feng
bullets: Targets the quadratic self-attention cost of high-resolution and long-duration video generation.
Uses size-weighted key/value centroids to estimate full normalized attention outputs coarsely.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse attention acceleration for video diffusion transformers with output-guided block selection; directly fits efficient attention and video diffusion.
papers.title: NOVA: Normalization-Aware Output-Guided Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: NOVA accelerates video diffusion transformer attention by selecting blocks based on their estimated impact on the normalized output, achieving higher fidelity and up to 1.82× end-to-end speedup.

papers.abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($\alpha=0$) and 98.83% at $\alpha=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $\alpha=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $\alpha=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
bullets: Addresses long-context retrieval degradation caused by attention normalization mass spreading across distractors.
Builds a linear-size local-window-plus-hub transport graph with sparsemax or thresholded-ReLU gating to eliminate excess distractor mass.
Adds annealed Sinkhorn updates, an exact low-rank adjoint, fused Triton kernels, and a causal chunked variant with zero future leakage.
At 262K tokens, sparsemax THOT achieves 97.40% or 98.83% fixed-binding recall depending on loss regularization, while softmax-gated hub OT reaches 3.52%.
Reports 100% multi-needle retrieval on 65K-token WikiText-103 queries and faster operator benchmarks than the compared baselines; broader multi-layer LM runs use an unfused path.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces hub optimal transport with sparse gating for long-context attention, directly targeting long-context models and efficient attention.
papers.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
papers.tldr: THOT uses sparse capacity-gated hub optimal transport and optimized kernels to preserve relevant facts in extremely long contexts while reducing attention overhead.

papers.abstract: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.
bullets: Soft anchor-routing pathways can produce highly redundant summaries, whereas exclusive patch partitions prevent collapse by construction.
The proposed focus anchors concentrate anchors near learned importance peaks while preserving exclusive Voronoi regions.
On CIFAR-100, exclusive routing is 2.4–3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention; focus anchors add 1.5 points on a cluttered canvas.
For full-HD traffic-sign recognition, both anchor variants match dense local-window attention at about one-fifth the FLOPs; fixed partitions train 1.5× faster per step.
Hard exclusive assignment was the most stable and accurate tested option, but anchors use more memory and do not outperform the trained ResNet-18 in this regime.

papers.selection_reason: Anchor-based routing with exclusive region assignment reduces attention cost in vision transformers, an efficient-attention contribution.
papers.title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Exclusive region assignment prevents anchor collapse in vision transformers, while focus-based placement can improve performance on cluttered scenes but is not universally beneficial.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.
authors: Hao Zhang, Bin Xiao, Kefeng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Sparse attention can reduce computation, but searching the entire visible history makes key retrieval a bottleneck for very long contexts.

Method: Partition history into independently indexed time buckets, organize keys into balanced directional groups, and use group centers for coarse page selection before refining candidates to select Top-K positions.
Implementation: Reordered pages, fused index-construction stages, shared fixed-candidate storage, and asynchronous index maintenance improve retrieval and inference efficiency.
Result: At 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection 4.70× over DSA and combined selection plus attention 35.60× over full attention.
Scope: The reported gains target long-context inference with incrementally arriving keys and prefix reuse.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA) to improve retrieval efficiency for long-context LLM inference.
papers.title: LongCat Recall Sparse Attention: Co-Designing Key Organization and Retrieval for Long-Context Inference
papers.tldr: LRSA makes long-context sparse attention substantially faster by co-designing an incrementally maintained, paged retrieval index with efficient GPU execution.

papers.abstract: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.
bullets: Shows a periodic sequence where every transition has spectral radius below one, yet the period product is expansive.
Extends the construction to sufficient conditions for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling.
Derives a necessary-and-sufficient spectral-norm criterion for channel-wise-decay rank-one erasure, computable in O(d) time.
The criterion matched direct SVD on all 1,800 tested operators.
In a Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base replay, terminal gain rose from 0.99938 to 1.3977 under repeated text with feature and gate trajectories fixed.

papers.title: Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure

papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
authors: Renjia Deng, Yuxi Liu, Yutong He, Xue Wang, Kun Yuan
bullets: Existing gated linear attention uses state-independent gates, which ignore the information currently stored in recurrent memory.
SDG computes element-wise gates from the memory change over each chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary.
The approach preserves parallel within-chunk computation and is implemented with fused kernels for several linear-attention architectures.
Theory connects SDG to improved signal reconstruction and interprets fixed-gate boundary decay as an element-wise ridge proximal step.
Experiments on 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens report improvements across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.
authors: Aoxiang Fan, Maria Pilligua, Corentin Dumery, Oliver Heinimann, Pascal Fua
bullets: Dense global attention scales quadratically with the number of views, limiting large-scale reconstruction.
A lightweight key-selection module predicts cross-view 3D proximity and selects only relevant patch tokens.
The approach can be integrated into different feed-forward reconstruction models through fine-tuning.
Experiments report the fastest runtime among compared dense and sparse methods, with the strongest accuracy among sparse methods.
At 1,000 views, SGAR runs up to 12× faster than dense attention while maintaining stable pose accuracy and producing more complete geometry under equal time budgets.

Figure 3. Overview of SGAR. We replace the global dense attention of DejaView [8] with our sparse geometric attention as an example. The images are encoded by DINOv2 and augmented with camera and register tokens. A single shared block, unrolled over its L steps, runs frame attention, key selection and sparse attention. In sparse attention, each patch attends to the special tokens of all views, the patches of the reference view, a summary of each cluster, and all the patches of the nearest clusters, so that its cost grows near-linearly with the number of views. Key Selection projects the patch tokens by Wadj into a geometric embedding and clusters the embeddings by spherical k-means into √ N clusters, re-clustered at every step. Each cluster probes its m = 4 nearest clusters, itself first. With the patches sorted by cluster, the selected keys form a block-sparse mask over tiles of 128 tokens. A contrastive loss pulls together the embeddings of patches that observe the same surface in the ground-truth geometry and pushes the others apart.

papers.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
authors: Ambroise Borbely, Mathieu Salzmann, Olivier Verscheure
bullets: Targets the full query-key dot product in LLM attention rather than sparsifying across tokens.
Uses a static, parameter-free rule based on token positions and RoPE structure to omit selected query/key components.
Preserves full query and key projections while computing only a partial attention score.
Training from scratch shows no performance loss and reported improvements over complete dot products.
Extends to FlashAttention-3 and reduces decoding time and memory usage; dense attention also learns to suppress the omitted components.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
authors: Emre U\u{g}ur, Jiawen Qi, Qinyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the prefill bottleneck of long-context attention, where accurately scoring skippable blocks can be costly.
Uses training-free, content-adaptive delta scoring with fewer anchors in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones.
Accelerates scoring through parallel, tile-aligned local scans, then computes selected tiles with the original vectors.
Maintains average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, including RULER up to 128K tokens.
Reports 38% lower scoring-pipeline latency than XAttention at 128K tokens and 3.3× prefill speedup over a FlashAttention-2 PyTorch baseline at 512K tokens on four H100 GPUs.
