papers.selection_reason: Proposes Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention, a method for closed-loop quality control in long-context decoding that improves efficiency through sparse attention mechanisms.
papers.title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: CVSA enables fast long-context sparse-attention decoding by verifying attention coverage and selectively correcting low-coverage heads, preserving near-dense quality.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but attention over long spatiotemporal sequences makes inference computationally expensive. Sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only a subset of query-key interactions exactly, and recent training-free methods further approximate the remaining interactions. These methods, however, degrade quickly at high sparsity, which limits the achievable speedup. We present ESTRA (Extreme Sparsity Through Refined Attention), a training-free acceleration method that preserves generation quality even at extreme sparsity. ESTRA concentrates exact attention computation on a small set of important key-value tokens and approximates the remaining contributions with cluster representatives. To identify these tokens efficiently, it groups similar queries and uses their representatives to score individual keys. A variance-based correction further refines the attention weights of the cluster representatives, improving the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B show that ESTRA establishes a new quality-efficiency frontier for training-free sparse attention, achieving $3.26\times$ and $4.71\times$ end-to-end speedups at 5% attention density while surpassing Sol-Attn and SVG-EAR in fidelity to dense generation and on most VBench dimensions. Even at 1% density, ESTRA remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5%, while reaching up to $5.39\times$ speedup.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over long spatiotemporal video sequences.
Selects a small set of important key-value tokens using clustered query representatives.
Approximates remaining attention with cluster representatives and applies variance-based weight correction.
At 5% attention density, achieves 3.26× and 4.71× end-to-end speedups on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B.
At 1% density, remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5% density, with up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.title: ESTRA: Enabling Extreme Attention Sparsity for Training-Free Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: ESTRA accelerates video diffusion transformers with training-free sparse attention, retaining high fidelity at extreme sparsity and delivering up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.abstract: A language model that never had to forget would keep every document it has read and every turn it has spoken, and answer from any of it. This paper shows that two stock models can do that on unmodified weights by manipulating their geometry. Rotary attention turns each pair of key dimensions, a plane, at its own rate. The slow planes turn once in thousands of tokens and carry the address a query matches when it reads a far key; the fast planes turn once in a few tokens, and the order of the tokens inside a span is already written into its keys and values by the time the span leaves the near window. At distance the position blurs, and what attention reads is a bag rather than a sequence. A far span is read by its words: under competition it is read only if it is visible at the query of the question's own handle word, and a read through a description rather than a word fails at distance in every model measured, a 70B included. These facts allow a trick. What sits in the far part of attention does not have to be the history as it was; it can be installed ahead of the prediction. The design keeps a near window of 8K tokens at their true positions and changes what lies beyond it with the prompt: every far key and value goes to the host exact, a word index finds the units the request's rare words name, a far window of slots inside the trained range holds them while the request is encoded, and a rare word the model generates fetches its units mid-generation with one exact re-encode. Implemented in llama.cpp on Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, the design reads planted single needles at 99 to 100 of 100 and three-key discrimination at 88 to 100 of 100 from 32K to one million tokens, scores 70.8 on RULER against 69.9 for dense attention on Llama-3.1-8B at 128K and 67.8 against 75.5 on Mistral-7B at 32K, and at 128K prefills at 1.85 times and decodes at 1.65 to 1.68 times stock speed.
bullets: Rotary attention preserves address-like information in slow dimensions but loses order for distant spans, making far-context retrieval largely word-based.
The method keeps the nearest 8K tokens at true positions and remaps distant keys and values into trained-range slots selected using rare query words.
During generation, rare generated words can trigger an exact re-encoding to retrieve additional relevant units.
On Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, it retrieved planted needles with 99–100/100 accuracy and achieved 88–100/100 on three-key discrimination from 32K to 1M tokens.
At 128K, it reported 1.85× faster prefilling and 1.65–1.68× faster decoding than stock speed, with task scores varying by model and benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Modifies attention geometry (rotary attention) to enable stock models to handle unbounded context (up to 1M tokens) with improved speed, contributing to efficient attention mechanisms.
papers.title: Retrofitting Unbounded Context onto Stock Language Models
papers.tldr: A prompt-driven KV-cache remapping strategy gives unmodified language models practical million-token context by preserving an 8K near window and selectively staging relevant far-away text.

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
authors: Dayou Du, Woon Yee Ng, Guangming Sheng, Nick Lau, Jianyi Cheng, Luo Mai
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Uses dual-residual query quantization, underflow-aware probability scaling, and outlier-aware key quantization to reduce FP4 accuracy loss.
Removes softmax overhead with transposed softmax, fused probability quantization, and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches.
Stays within 0.5 accuracy points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 and within 1 point with MXFP4 across dense and MoE models.
On NVIDIA B300, achieves 2.4–3.0× higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV for Qwen3 models.

papers.selection_reason: Algorithm-system co-design for native FP4 KV cache decoding, directly targeting KV cache memory and inference efficiency.
papers.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
papers.tldr: BitDecoding-FP4 co-designs quantization algorithms and GPU kernels to enable accurate, native FP4 KV-cache decoding with up to 3.0× higher serving throughput than BF16 KV.

papers.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
bullets: Targets decode attention, where quantized KV caches reduce memory traffic but can remain latency-bound by dequantization overhead.
Uses affine folding tailored to token-wise or channel-wise quantization, preserving the exact dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic.
Employs bit manipulation and warp-specialized Hopper/Blackwell GPU pipelines to efficiently feed quantized operands to Tensor Cores.
Reports substantial kernel speedups on H100 and B200 against BF16, FP8, and, in some cases, NVFP4 baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves peak aggregate throughput on long-context serving workloads by up to 170% versus 2-bit and 341% versus 16-bit baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a kernel-level technique for accelerating decode attention over quantized KV caches, directly addressing KV cache memory and inference efficiency.
papers.title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding
papers.tldr: FOSCAR accelerates 2- and 4-bit KV-cache decode attention by folding quantization scales and offsets into matrix operations instead of dequantizing each value.

papers.abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
authors: Wajih Hassan Raza, Ahsan Bilal, Yidan Shen, Renjie Hu, Xin Fu, Yu Wen
bullets: Targets the computational and KV-memory bottleneck of attention as context length grows.
Uses each head’s query-key operator to determine an effective feature rank and compact response space.
Merges neighboring token regions when their responses are directionally coherent, while preserving heterogeneous regions separately.
Computes exact attention with original full-dimensional KV states for selected regions.
Captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass, improves reported RULER and LongBench-Pro accuracy over UNIQUE by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points, and reaches up to 14.07× speedup over dense attention.

papers.title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure

papers.abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.
authors: Tianxing Wu, Juuso Korhonen, Jesus Carabano Bravo
bullets: Addresses softmax as the bottleneck preventing attention from exploiting rapidly increasing low-precision matrix throughput.
Introduces a training-free approximation that folds dominant softmax operations into attention GEMMs.
On AMD CDNA 4, MXFP8/6/4 kernels achieve about 3.0/4.0/4.6 PFLOP/s and 2.1×/2.8×/3.2× speedups over BF16 attention.
A hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule provides up to 2.05× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B without degrading visual quality.
Implemented in AMD’s open-source AITER library and used in an MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of InstaGen. (a) Queries and keys are clustered into groups. (b) Centroid scores give each key group a probability π of being used by each query group. (c) The top key group is always kept; the remaining keys are sampled in proportion to π and weighted by 1/π. (d) Queries in a group share the same keys, so attention runs over dense blocks in one kernel.

papers.title: InstaGen: Group-Shared Importance Sampling for Fast Video Generation
papers.tldr: InstaGen accelerates video diffusion by replacing inefficient top-block selection with group-shared importance sampling, improving reconstruction quality at comparable compute.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
bullets: GDN-2’s erasure updates are less sensitive than value writes, motivating lower-rank, sensitivity-allocated gating.
Muir fuses gates into a low-rank projection and re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout to reduce interference from high-norm, slow-decaying rows.
A numerically stable parallel update enables efficient training with the large chunks needed for wide matrix units.
Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir reduces perplexity versus GDN-2 and Transformer, improves commonsense accuracy and extractive recall, and matches GDN-2 throughput.
At 1.34B, it supports long-context extrapolation to 10M tokens and near-perfect passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Muir outperforms GDN-2 and Transformer on language modeling and long-context throughput while improving recall over GDN-2. (a) Sensitivity-allocated low-rank gates with FFN expansion drive the bulk of the validation NLL gain over GDN-2, while dynamic matched-filter readout drives the gain on extractive recall. (b) Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir lowers validation NLL by 18.0–20.4 millinats over GDN-2 and 25.0–36.2 millinats over Transformer. (c) On 8 TPU7x chips (0.5M tokens/step) at 1.34B with our chunkwise kernel, Muir matches GDN-2 throughput despite an additional readout gate and a 30.4% wider FFN, and trains 1.64× and 2.74× faster than Transformer at 16K and 32K, respectively.

Figure 6 |Muir improves synthetic single-needle, multi-hop, multi-needle, and real-world retrieval over GDN-2. (a) Averaged across the three single-needle tasks, all Muir variants mitigate the 4K degradation of GDN-2 and extrapolate to 8K, where unextended RoPE Transformer degrades beyond its 4K training window. (b) On 5-hop variable-binding chains, static 𝛾 fails to match the varying hop lags, whereas dynamic 𝛾𝑡 leads all models at every context length. (c, d) When retrieving four values bound to a single key or four distinct keys queried jointly, dynamic 𝛾𝑡 matches or outperforms both GDN-2 and Transformer across 1K–4K. (e) Averaged across the RULER tasks (a–d) by needle depth and context length, Muir achieves the largest gains over GDN-2 on early needles (0–40% depth) at 4K–8K. (f) On real-world document extraction at 2K, Muir improves over GDN-2 on all six tasks, with dynamic 𝛾𝑡 driving 69% of the gain.

(b) On the 256× 256 MXU, an unfused 256 × 128 right-hand side 𝑉 achieves only 50% utilization due to zero-padded lanes, whereas the fused solve [︀ 𝑈 𝑌 ]︀ = 𝑇−1 [︀𝑉 ?̂?⊙𝜋 ]︀ achieves 100% utilization. (d) Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution combines pre-permutation VREG fusion for 𝑞𝑡 and 𝑣𝑡, MXU cumulative log-decay, numerically stable VPU decay splitting, recursive block inversion of 𝑇 on the MXU, and a packed MXU scan carrying 𝑆0 → 𝑆𝐶 in VMEM (saving 𝑆0 only for backward).

(a) Standard residual block with a Muir token mixer. (b) Within the Muir block, 𝑥𝑡 feeds linear-Conv-SiLU pathways for (𝑞𝑡,𝑘𝑡,𝑣𝑡) alongside a single fused low-rank gate projection that produces all five gates (log𝛼𝑡, 𝑏𝑡, 𝑔𝑡,𝑤𝑡,𝛾𝑡). papers.selection_reason: Linear attention architecture with gating and matched-filter readout; contributes to efficient attention and LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
papers.tldr: Muir improves gated linear attention by allocating gate capacity according to update sensitivity and using matched-filter state readout, achieving better language modeling, recall, and long-context performance at similar or lower training cost.

papers.abstract: Self-attention carries a quadratic cost in token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers can scale with input resolution. We introduce SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians spatial operator that replaces dense self-attention with a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing the per-layer cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to subquadratic in $N$. Unlike dot-product self-attention, whose Lipschitz constant is unbounded outside a compact input domain, SSoG with fixed kernels is globally Lipschitz continuous, which, via the Picard--Lindelöf theorem, guarantees that the continuous-depth variant has a unique solution on the whole integration interval, a global guarantee that dense-attention counterparts lack in general. On CIFAR-100 at $224\times224$, in a matched discrete-Transformer setting and in the continuous setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2--4.1 points across three model widths while using 8.8--16.6\% fewer parameters, with depth and training recipe held fixed. In a looped-Transformer setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.4--8.1 points. We further probe inference-time scaling by evaluating on inputs up to $1024\times1024$ at matched batch size: in the continuous-depth (Neural ODE) architecture, SSoG reaches up to 154\% higher throughput and over 60\% lower peak memory than dense attention, with the gap widening as resolution grows, consistent with the difference in asymptotic cost. In the discrete and looped settings, SSoG also achieves over 30\% higher throughput than dense attention at this resolution. Together, these results establish SSoG as a practical, parameter-efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared, and continuous-depth Transformer variants.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic token-cost bottleneck of dense self-attention at high image resolutions.
Uses a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing per-layer complexity to subquadratic in the token count.
With fixed kernels, SSoG is globally Lipschitz, supporting unique whole-interval solutions for its continuous-depth Neural ODE formulation.
On CIFAR-100, it improves Top-1 accuracy across discrete, continuous, and looped Transformer settings while using fewer parameters.
At up to 1024×1024 resolution, it delivers substantially higher throughput and lower peak memory than dense attention, especially in the continuous-depth model.

papers.abstract: Head pose estimation is important for human computer interaction and driver monitoring, but many image based methods remain too costly for resource constrained deployment. We propose STAG-Net, a structure-aware attention over landmark groups for lightweight head Pose estimation that estimates head pose from facial landmarks using movement aware selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self attention, and a global geometry descriptor. We develop variants using FaceMesh and Face Alignment Network landmarks and evaluate them under cross dataset and subject independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI. STAG-Net achieves the lowest mean absolute error among all compared landmark based methods in every evaluated setting. On BIWI frames with valid detections, the FAN variant also records the lowest overall error among all compared methods, reaching $3.51^\circ$ under cross dataset evaluation and $2.39^\circ$ under subject independent evaluation. The regressors use only 0.012 to 0.043 million parameters and 24.1 to 83.6 thousand FLOPs, about three orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs than FSA-Net. Despite including landmark extraction and regression, the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 frames per second on a Tesla T4 GPU, nearly twice the 164.5 frames per second of the fastest measured image based baseline, and 111.0 frames per second on CPU. After normalization by dataset size, STAG-Net processes training samples seven to eight times faster than FSA-Net and more than one hundred times faster than HopeNet and TokenHPE, while complete training finishes within 28 minutes. These results show that STAG-Net combines leading landmark based accuracy with substantially lower training and inference cost.
bullets: Targets efficient head pose estimation for resource-constrained human–computer interaction and driver-monitoring systems.
Combines movement-aware landmark selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self-attention, and a global geometry descriptor.
Evaluated with FaceMesh and FAN landmarks under cross-dataset and subject-independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI.
Achieves the lowest mean absolute error among compared landmark-based methods in every setting, with the FAN variant reaching 3.51° and 2.39° on BIWI under the two protocols.
Uses 0.012–0.043M parameters and 24.1–83.6K FLOPs; the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 FPS on a Tesla T4 and 111.0 FPS on CPU.

papers.abstract: Linear attention reduces the quadratic sequence-length complexity of softmax attention by maintaining fixed-size recurrent states. However, these states scale quadratically with the representation dimension and require repeated data transfers during decoding, creating a substantial GPU memory bottleneck. Recent studies have revealed significant low-rank redundancy in recurrent states, suggesting opportunities for more efficient representations. We introduce SPARE (State Projection for Accelerated Recurrent Execution), a training-free method that exploits this redundancy through fixed low-dimensional subspaces, heterogeneous rank allocation, and lightweight write compensation. By performing recurrent reads and updates directly on compact states, SPARE reduces memory traffic without online decomposition or dense-state reconstruction. SPARE achieves 2.55x full-model decoding speedup, 7.49x lower recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, and 3.31x lower peak GPU memory, while preserving better associative-retrieval accuracy than structured pruning at matched memory budgets.
bullets: Addresses quadratic-in-representation-dimension recurrent states and repeated GPU data transfers in linear attention.
Uses fixed low-dimensional subspaces, heterogeneous rank allocation, and lightweight write compensation.
Performs recurrent reads and updates directly on compact states without online decomposition or dense-state reconstruction.
Reports 2.55× faster full-model decoding, 7.49× lower recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, and 3.31× lower peak GPU memory.
Preserves better associative-retrieval accuracy than structured pruning at matched memory budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Ablation studies of the key design choices in SPARE. All panels report associative retrieval accuracy on 512 four-choice prompts, with 256 prompts each at retrieval depths of 64 and 128. (a) Heterogeneous rank allocation. We compare SPARE with Uniform SPARE at matched recurrent-state budgets of 6, 9, and 12 MiB. Both methods use the same Key-PCA basis construction and write-compensation mechanism, differing only in how ranks are distributed across layers and heads. Heterogeneous allocation consistently achieves higher retrieval accuracy. (b) Subspace construction. We compare Key-based, State-based, and Value-based PCA projections under a fixed 12 MiB state budget, matched calibration data, and identical per-head rank allocations. Key and State PCA use right-side projections, whereas Value PCA uses a left-side projection. Key-side write compensation is disabled for this comparison and is not applicable to the Value-side formulation. Key PCA achieves the highest retrieval accuracy among the evaluated subspaces. (c) Write compensation. We compare SPARE-H32 and SPARE-H64 with and without projected-Key write compensation, holding their respective rank allocations and projection bases fixed. Enabling compensation improves retrieval accuracy at both compression budgets. All state budgets refer to persistent recurrent-state storage per request rather than peak GPU memory.

Figure 3: Decoding efficiency and memory savings of SPARE. We evaluate SPARE-H32 and SPARE-H64 against the Dense Gated DeltaNet baseline across batch sizes of 32, 128, and 512. (a) Full-model decoding speedup relative to Dense. (b) Reduction in recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, measured using hardware counters and normalized by the corresponding Dense kernels. (c) Reduction in peak GPU memory, computed as the ratio of Dense to SPARE peak memory usage during full-model inference. Experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs using stateful CUDA Graph decoding. The results demonstrate that compact recurrent states reduce memory traffic and GPU memory requirements while accelerating full-model decoding.

Figure 2: Quality–memory trade-off of recurrent-state compression. We compare SPARE with DRRQR structured pruning across different compression budgets. (a) Next-token NLL on WikiText-103 (lower is better). (b) Associative retrieval accuracy over 512 four-choice prompts (higher is better). (c) Mean accuracy across three selected downstream tasks: SQuAD Completion, TriviaQA, and DROP (higher is better). Peak GPU memory is measured during full-model inference with batch size 512, a prefill length of 128 tokens, and 64 decoding steps. Across these evaluations, SPARE provides a favorable quality–memory trade-off, particularly under aggressive compression.

State denotes persistent recurrent-state storage per request, excluding model weights and other runtime memory. Bold values indicate the better result within each matched-budget comparison.

papers.abstract: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zyphra/zyfa.
bullets: Targets long-context attention, where softmax limits the benefits of FP8 matrix throughput on MI355X.
Uses direct FP8 probability computation, ping-pong overlap of softmax and matrix multiplication, and power-of-two probability scaling before rounding.
Achieves 1.16–1.76× AITER throughput on inputs from three models at sustained clock speeds.
On 32K-token Gaussian benchmarks, reaches 1.26–1.37× speedup at head dimension 128 and 1.99× for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.
At head dimension 128, numerical error is within a few percent of Composable Kernel and Triton, and 62–78% lower than AITER’s.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Thread traces showing that AITER’s FP8 kernel leaves the matrix pipe idle while its waves compute exponentials and wait at barriers, and that ZYFA’s FP8 kernel keeps the matrix pipe busy most of the time. A thread trace records every instruction that a wave issues, cycle by cycle, here with the thread-trace mode of AMD’s rocprofv3 profiler. Each panel shows the two waves that share one SIMD over 2500 cycles in the middle of the loop over key blocks, where every block repeats the same work, in the FP8 kernels at dqk=128 (S=8K tokens, H=32 heads, multi-head attention). Each wave row shows the class of each instruction that the wave issues, and the matrix-pipe row below it shows when that wave’s MFMAs run. A vector instruction runs on the vector pipe during its bar in the wave row, so the wave rows already show when the vector pipe works. An MFMA keeps running on the matrix pipe for 32 to 64 cycles after its short bar in the wave row, while the wave issues other instructions, so the matrix-pipe rows show that work separately.

Fig. 16: Output error of one attention call for every layer of each model, as relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs (lower is more accurate). The inputs are the q, k, and v that each model produces on the first 4095 tokens of WikiText-2 (S=4K). The FP8 row uses a logarithmic axis.

Fig. 5: Scaling each block of probabilities before rounding keeps them in the range where FP8 is accurate, and dividing by the sum of the same rounded values keeps the attention weights summing to one. The schematic shows the probabilities p of one query row by 64-key block. (1) AITER’s FP8 kernel rounds p to e4m3 relative to the row maximum. Blocks more than 6 binades (factors of two) below the maximum become subnormal, with fewer significant bits, and values more than 10 binades below underflow to zero in the numerator. The row sum adds the unrounded p in FP32. (2) ZYFA multiplies each block by 2o so that its largest probability gets the same e4m3 value as p=1, and the scaled matrix instruction (MFMA) that computes PV divides the factor out at no cost. The numerator and the row sum use the same rounded values p̂. The P error is the relative error that rounding p adds to the attention output on Mistral-7B (Figure 20).

Fig. 1: Throughput of ZYFA and AITER’s default kernels on the queries, keys, and values captured from one layer per model at sequence length 16K, timed at sustained clocks (the steady clock after warmup launches). L20 is layer 20. The label above each pair is AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time. Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B have head dimension 128, where the FP8 kernel uses lean P, which writes each FP8 probability with one multiply-add instead of an exponential. DeepSeekV2-Lite has the MLA shape, where the FP8 kernel uses exact P, which evaluates the exponential (Section IV-B), and AITER uses Composable Kernel (CK) in FP8 and its OPUS kernel, written with AITER’s C++ template library, in BF16. Table X gives the clock of these runs.

Fig. 8: Throughput of ZYFA and AITER against sequence length on Gaussian inputs (random q, k, and v with standard deviation 0.1). Lean P rounds y from Equation 2 (with shift σ=6 and bias β=0.35) to the nearest integer and uses it as the e4m3 bit pattern, and the dashed line is the error of y before rounding. Fig. 25: Occupancy of the compute units (CUs) of the GPU over time for one attention layer (schematic). TABLE I: Properties of one MI355X from [Advanced Micro Devices, 2025b,a]. The peaks assume the maximum clock. VGPRs are the vector registers of a wave, XCDs are the eight chiplets, and LDS is the shared memory of a compute unit (CU). Our system caps the board power at the TBP.

TABLE III: In FP8 the softmax needs about as many vectorpipe cycles as the matrix products need matrix-pipe cycles, so the two must overlap almost perfectly to keep the matrix pipe busy, while in BF16 the matrix products take more than twice as long as the softmax. The table gives pipe cycles for one wave (a group of 64 threads) that computes 32 queries against one 128-key block at dqk=dv=128, and each of its 64 lanes holds 64 of the 4096 scores. Matrix cycles, on the pipe that runs matrix (MFMA) instructions, follow from the matrix rate per cycle, and vector cycles, on the pipe that runs elementwise instructions, follow from the measured costs in Section III-A. Exact P, the standard method, evaluates the exponential and converts the result to e4m3 or BF16, and the packed BF16 conversion occupies the vector pipe for 4 cycles instead of 8. Lean P, ZYFA’s method, writes the e4m3 bit pattern of each probability with one multiply-add and one integer conversion (Section IV-B1). Rescaling the output adds vector work when the row maximum grows.

TABLE X: ZYFA and AITER on one layer per model at S=16K (Mistral-7B layer 20, Qwen3-8B layer 18, DeepSeekV2-Lite layer 13). The captured columns use the q, k, and v that the model produces on WikiText-2 text, and the Gaussian columns use random inputs of the same shape. Each run launches one kernel back to back for seconds and is timed only after the GPU clock has settled (sustained clocks). The time ratio is AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time, so values above 1 mean that ZYFA takes less time. SCLK is the shader clock of the slowest of the eight chiplets, which sets the kernel time.

TABLE XIII: Effect of rotating Q and K with a Hadamard matrix (rotation) and of subtracting the mean key of each head (K smoothing) before FP8 quantization, for all-FP8 ZYFA attention. The error of one call is the relative RMS error of the attention output O against fp64 attention, from quantizing the inputs alone (input) and in total. KL is the per-token KL divergence from the model with BF16 attention, and dNLL the change in negative log-likelihood per token, both on the 48 PG-19 evaluation documents. Times are relative to all-FP8 attention without transforms. The fused column includes one quantization pass that also applies the transforms. The separate column runs the transforms as PyTorch operations and includes no quantization. The last column is the time of the separate transforms per forward pass at 16K.

TABLE XIV: How well each score chooses the units (heads, 128-row blocks, or layers) that run in BF16. Each value is the KL divergence from the BF16 model that remains when the top 5, 10, or 20% of units by the score run in BF16, divided by the KL divergence of all-FP8 attention (lower is better), on 12 evaluation documents per model with the exact-P build of ZYFA’s FP8 kernel. The local-error oracle ranks units by the true FP8 error of their own attention output. ge2 ranks heads by their gradient-weighted error g2e2, and layer KL ranks layers by how much FP8 attention in that layer alone changes the output of the model. Both use calibration documents (Section VI-C), and the scores below the rule are computed at inference time. A row block has 128 query rows, and its BF16 share of the causal work differs slightly from the nominal share. On the 48 documents of Figure 24 with lean P, ge2 and layer KL give values within 0.02 of these.
TABLE II: Terms used throughout the paper.

TABLE V: Under sustained load the MFMA loops run below the 2.4GHz clock that the datasheet peaks assume, so each reaches less than its datasheet throughput. The table gives empirical peaks, the sustained throughput of microbenchmark loops on all 256 compute units (CUs) with two waves per SIMD and operands that change every instruction, over about 2.5 s of back-to-back launches. The columns give the shader clock (SCLK) in GHz, the board power in kW, and the throughput in PFLOP/s. The synthetic attention loop has the per-tile counts of MFMAs, reads from the on-chip shared memory (LDS), loads into it (DMA), and barriers of ZYFA’s FP8 kernel at dqk=128. The BF16 rows use v_mfma_f32_32x32x16_bf16 and v_mfma_f32_16x16x32_bf16, the FP8 rows v_mfma_f32_32x32x64_f8f6f4 and v_mfma_f32_16x16x128_f8f6f4 with e4m3 operands, and the FP4 row v_mfma_f32_16x16x128_f8f6f4 with FP4 operands, all in their unscaled forms. The datasheet peaks assume 2.4GHz.

TABLE VI: Configurations that the ZYFA kernels support. MHA is multi-head attention and GQA grouped-query attention, in which Hq/Hkv query heads share each key-value head. BHSD and BSHD give the order of the batch, head, sequence, and head-dimension axes in memory, M and N are the numbers of queries and keys, and LSE is the log-sum-exp of each row of scores.

TABLE IV: Both kernels keep the vector pipe about as busy as the matrix pipe, and neither overlaps the two fully. The table gives pipe cycles per SIMD at S=32K for FP8 multi-head attention at dqk=128, for two units of work of one wave on 32 queries and 64 keys each, which together equal the work of one wave on one 128-key block in Table III. AITER is AITER’s FP8 assembly kernel. Base is an earlier HIP version of ZYFA’s FP8 kernel with a Schraudolph exponential (an exponential that writes the bits of an FP32 number directly from the score) and an FP32 row sum, and its instruction mix comes from S=8K traces. The matrix row includes the cycles in which packed FP32 instructions block the matrix pipe, given in parentheses. The serialized row is the sum of matrix and vector cycles, which the work would take if the two never overlapped, and the achieved row gives the cycles that each kernel actually takes. TABLE IX: Throughput of ZYFA divided by that of AITER’s default kernel at batch sizes B=1 and B=4, for multi-head attention on Gaussian inputs, kernel-only. Values above 1 mean that ZYFA takes less time.
TABLE XVII: Heads of DeepSeek-V2-Lite with the largest ge2 score (gradient-weighted FP8 error), with the columns of Table XV.

Qwen3-8B’s documents have no BOS token, so its key 0 is the first text token. The mean distance between query and key is weighted by attention and given in tokens, and the entropy of the attention row is given in nats. papers.selection_reason: FP8 FlashAttention kernels with improved throughput and numerical accuracy, a direct contribution to efficient attention.
papers.title: ZYFA: Speed and Accuracy of FP8 FlashAttention on AMD CDNA4
papers.tldr: ZYFA accelerates FP8 attention prefill on AMD MI355X by redesigning softmax computation and scheduling, delivering higher throughput with competitive numerical accuracy.

papers.abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.
bullets: Targets the differing precision and retention sensitivities of query-key interactions in long-context attention.
Uses two diagonal-distance boundaries per head to compactly define skipped, 4-bit, and 8-bit computation regions.
Calibrates boundary choices with projected-output error and tile execution cost, then allocates policies across heads under a shared budget.
Employs a fused prefill kernel and reuses quantized keys and values in a compressed KV cache during decoding.
Reports up to 7.88× speedup over Torch attention and 2.65× over BF16, with quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TriAttention, a unified sparse mixed-precision attention mechanism for long-context LLM inference. It optimizes computation by assigning different precision levels (4-bit vs 8-bit) to different tiles based on sensitivity.
papers.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TriAttention accelerates long-context LLM inference by jointly skipping attention tiles and assigning retained tiles 4-bit or 8-bit precision while preserving model quality.

papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
bullets: Builds a hierarchical KV-cache tree whose nodes summarize subtrees with pooled keys and values.
Selects at most k candidates per level, reducing per-query selection and reads to O(log L).
Uses shared, dense-attention-distilled poolers and level-relative RoPE positions to support length extrapolation.
Outperforms reported baselines from 131K to 2M tokens; at 1M, scores 60.5 versus 40.0 for Dense + DCA on RULER.
With optimized kernels, achieves 3.2× prefill and 3.8× decoding speedups at 524K on one H200 GPU.

papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
authors: Jo\~ao Eduardo Batista, Emil Vatai, Mohamed Wahib
bullets: Targets full-attention layers that remain costly at long contexts in hybrid models.
Combines a recent-token sliding window, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of salient context tokens.
Uses per-layer multi-objective search to select the window size and token budget without changing weights.
Across six models and 21 long-context datasets, configurations preserve baseline accuracy.
Provides up to 2.22× faster decoding at 256k tokens, depending on the model.

papers.abstract: High-content multi-channel imaging, from Cell Painting assays to remote sensing, is central to modern scientific pipelines. Because these channels are highly heterogeneous and experimental configurations frequently evolve, a practical vision backbone must be fundamentally channel-agnostic. Current channel-adaptive vision transformers rely on global self-attention with learnable channel embeddings, which can be computed only for previously known channels. Attempts to overcome this limitation of new channels either discard the embeddings, losing channel identity, or process each channel independently, thereby eliminating critical cross-channel interactions. To address this, we introduce ChanSFormer, an efficient Vision Transformer that replaces rigid embeddings with disentangled spatial-channel attention and individual channel CLS tokens. This architecture natively preserves both distinct channel identities and cross-channel information flow. Furthermore, the individual channel class token design unlocks more informative feature representations for self-supervised learning and enables representation-based channel sampling while remaining channel-agnostic. We evaluate ChanSFormer on two biology multi-channel datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP and a satellite dataset, So2Sat. Experimental results show that ChanSFormer outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3.93%-4.27% on JUMP-CP in classification accuracy. It also demonstrates exceptional cross-dataset transferability under a self-supervised setting, outperforming previous methods by up to 2.72% in accuracy in the same classification tasks. Furthermore, the disentangled attention reduces the quadratic complexity of channel-by-spatial sequence length of the global attention baseline, thus improving throughput by 55%-313%. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/ChanSFormer.
authors: Jingwei Zhang, Srinivasan Sivanandan, Dimitris Samaras
bullets: Addresses the limitation of channel-adaptive transformers that depend on predefined channel embeddings and handle new channels poorly.

Supports more informative self-supervised representations and representation-based channel sampling.
Evaluated on CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat; on JUMP-CP, it improves classification accuracy by 3.93–4.27% over state-of-the-art methods and improves cross-dataset transfer by up to 2.72%.
Reduces attention complexity and improves throughput by 55–313% compared with global attention baselines.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates few-step video diffusion transformers by computing a few key blocks exactly and compensating for the rest. However, existing sparse attention still faces key challenges, including identification overhead from finding critical blocks at every denoising step, suboptimal budget allocation that sets sparsity budgets uniformly or by local metrics, and cross-step error accumulation as reused masks or clusters go stale. Observing that the errors left on skipped blocks cancel each other once every key is compensated, we propose DecoupAttn, a new paradigm of decoupled sparse attention: semantic clusters compensate every key, and exact attention corrects their error on a few blocks fixed once offline by position. To support this paradigm, we introduce Distortion Budget, a rate-distortion objective for budget allocation that places exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads where it removes the most distortion that compensation leaves in the final latent. Built on this budget, we further propose Reassign Cache, in which each step reassigns the drifting keys to cached centroids and refreshes compensation while the budgeted blocks stay fixed. Moreover, DecoupAttn is training-free: a few calibration clips compile one plan offline, and inference runs standard block-sparse kernels with one fused compensation kernel. Our code will be released after submission.
authors: Yanjin Li, Bingbing Qiu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanfeng Li, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang, Mingda Zhang
bullets: Targets identification overhead, poor uniform/local budget allocation, and stale masks or clusters in sparse video diffusion attention.
Uses semantic clusters to compensate skipped keys and exact attention on a small set of offline-fixed blocks to correct residual error.
Introduces Distortion Budget to allocate exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads based on its effect on final-latent distortion.
Uses Reassign Cache to update drifting key-to-centroid assignments and refresh compensation at each denoising step.
Compiles the plan from a few calibration clips and performs inference with block-sparse kernels plus one fused compensation kernel; no training is required.

papers.selection_reason: Decoupled sparse attention with distortion-budget allocation for training-free acceleration of video diffusion, directly relevant to efficient attention and video diffusion.
papers.title: DecoupAttn: Decoupled Sparse Attention for Training-Free Acceleration of Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: DecoupAttn accelerates video diffusion without retraining by combining fixed exact-attention blocks, semantic compensation, and distortion-aware sparse-budget allocation.

papers.abstract: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.
authors: Xinhang Zhang, Boning Zhang, Chengchun Liu, Chunpu Li, Lei Sun, Weifeng Zhang, Limin Xiao
bullets: Targets poor GPU utilization from communication dependencies in sequence-parallel attention, especially under cross-hardware bandwidth imbalance.
Uses hierarchical sequential communication to enable intra-level parallelism and overlap communication with computation.
Decouples cross-hardware and intra-hardware communication to remove synchronization overhead caused by unequal bandwidth.
Evaluated forward and backward attention across multiple hardware architectures, outperforming prior methods.
Against Ring-Attention, reports 1.3×/1.7× average forward/backward speedups on dual-NUMA PCIe and 2.8×/2.9× on dual-node NVLink.

(a) displays parallel communication of q is first performed across NUMA. As a result, GPU 3 receives the q from GPU 7, eliminating the need for further cross-NUMA communication. (b) shows the parallel communication and computation of q and kv. In this step, GPU 3 communicates q with GPU 0 and kv with GPU 1. After completing the computation of Q0,4, GPU3 communicates back to GPU 0 and receives the output. (c) performs the last step of RM+, where GPU 3 only communicates kv with GPU 2. (d) shows that once all kv results are computed, the output is communicated back to GPU 7. (e) illustrates the overall cross-NUMA communication and the full overlap of computation and communication of GPU3 happened in (a)-(d).

Each intra-pipeline processes queries (Q) from other pipelines and uses the same workflow with its local KV, returning the final out back. Effective overlap allows inter-pipeline communication to be hidden by intra-pipeline, further improving performance.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CHARM+, a method to optimize cross-hardware attention in LLMs by reorganizing communication and decoupling cross-hardware synchronization, directly addressing efficiency bottlenecks in distributed attention.
papers.title: CHARM+: Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism
papers.tldr: CHARM+ accelerates distributed attention across heterogeneous hardware by restructuring communication for greater overlap and less synchronization.

papers.abstract: Expert offloading enables large mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models to run locally, but conventional batching stalls the GPU while missing experts are fetched. A popular remedy, known as prefetching, is to predict what experts will be needed soon and fetch them using idle link bandwidth. Imprecise prediction, however, wastes bandwidth and GPU memory on fetching unnecessary experts. Our key finding is that prefetching can be harmful when there is an expert cache in GPU memory. This is because as the cache includes more necessary experts, expert prediction becomes less precise. Our key insight is that proper request scheduling beats prefetching. Building on this insight, we present Bevy, an MoE inference system based on runahead inference for concurrent requests. A request whose experts are available can run ahead to later layers while other requests wait for fetches, revealing the experts it needs next. Bevy can then fetch the missing experts so identified while computing ready requests, overlapping computation and fetching without predicting expert selections. Running requests separately, however, repeats reads of shared weights in GPU memory and increases compute time. To limit this cost, Bevy's self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests at each layer and prioritizes lagging requests, adapting their grouping as expert availability changes. Across two local platforms, Bevy delivers up to 3.46$\times$ the decode throughput of llama.cpp and up to 1.55$\times$ that of the fastest prefetching baseline.
authors: Hongseung Yu, In Gim, Kyunghan Lee, Lin Zhong
bullets: Expert offloading can stall GPU execution when required experts must be fetched.
Prefetching may waste bandwidth and GPU memory because larger expert caches reduce prediction precision.
Bevy uses runahead inference: requests with available experts advance to reveal future needs while others wait.
A self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests and prioritizes lagging requests to reduce repeated weight reads and computation.
Across two local platforms, Bevy achieves up to 3.46× the decode throughput of llama.cpp and 1.55× that of the fastest prefetching baseline.

Figure 8. Throughput as the number of concurrent requests grows. The numbers above the bars give Bevy’s speedup over the fastest baseline. Even without prefetching, Bevy achieves the highest throughput in every configuration.

Figure 7. Operation of opportunistic layerwise grouping. (a) With many misses, only R2 is ready when R1 finishes, so R2 runs alone. (b) With few misses, R2, R3, and R4 are all ready and run together as one batch.

(b) Same as (a), but predicted experts are prefetched during computation. Because prediction is never perfect, prefetching unnecessary experts wastes both bandwidth and GPU memory. (c) Each request runs without waiting for the other’s fetches, so fetches overlap with computation.

Figure 11. Mean step time against the number of missing experts per step, for static groupings and Bevy’s opportunistic layerwise grouping. Which static grouping is fastest depends on the number of missing experts, while Bevy achieves the lowest step time at every point by adapting groups to the missing experts at each layer.
Figure 5. Accumulated extra misses over the mean for four concurrent requests ranked by their misses in layers 0–3 (Qwen3.6-35BA3B, ShareGPT, 30% expert cache).

Figure 10. (a) Step time split by whether the link and the GPU are busy or idle. (b) Expert fetches per step: missing experts fetched on demand, and prefetched experts that the step needed or wasted. Bevy keeps the link and the GPU busy together for most of the step while fetching only the experts that the requests need.

Prefetching does not improve the throughput of Bevy: with few requests, many prefetches are wasted, and with more requests, the link has no idle time left for prefetching.

Figure 12. (a) Change in GPU busy time, GPU idle time, and step time relative to Bevy when the fetch order, the compute order, or both are changed. (b) Share of groups by group size, the number of jobs that run together as one batch. Lowest-layer-first compute ordering creates batching opportunities: it forms larger groups, and the GPU busy time it saves outweighs the increase in GPU idle time.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Bevy, a system for accelerating MoE inference by interleaving concurrent requests and using a self-balancing scheduler. This addresses inference efficiency and optimization, fitting the Efficient AI subtopic.
papers.title: Accelerating Offloading-Based MoE Inference by Interleaving Concurrent Requests
papers.tldr: Bevy accelerates local MoE inference by scheduling concurrent requests to overlap expert fetching with computation, avoiding inaccurate prefetch predictions.

papers.abstract: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers. In particular, we analyze the unequal relevance of attention-matrix columns to the final computation and show that this phenomenon becomes increasingly pronounced with network depth. This can be interpreted as saying that tokens have an absolute importance for the attention process, independently of queries. Inspired by this, we propose a reformulation of the attention formula that makes this phenomenon explicit by adding an input-dependent bias to the query-key dot product. We show that this new term gives each token a scalar value indicating its anticipated influence on other tokens during the attention process, and can thus serve as a proxy for pruning attention maps. Across multiple transformer model sizes, this allows us to substantially reduce the computational cost of attention, in terms of both FLOPs and inference latency, while retaining most of the original classification accuracy. We publicly released the code and models at https://github.com/EIDOSLAB/AttentionWithBias.
authors: Charles Herr, Gabriele Spadaro, Enzo Tartaglione
bullets: Attention-matrix columns contribute unequally to the final computation, with this imbalance increasing at greater network depth.
The method adds an input-dependent bias to query–key dot products to estimate each token’s anticipated influence on others.
These scalar token scores act as a proxy for pruning attention maps.
Across multiple transformer sizes, pruning substantially reduces attention FLOPs and inference latency while retaining most classification accuracy.
Code and models are publicly released.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Cone Alignment Index (CAI), a scale-invariant sparsity measure associated with a Lorentz-cone geometry. We provide a probabilistic analysis of the distribution of the CAI score, including a general theorem and explicit corollaries for Gaussian and uniform distributions. As a consequence, we show that, in the high-sparsity regime, the probability that the samples lie within the convex cone tends to one. Building upon this formulation, we derive two complementary projections: the \emph{Parametric Linear Conic Projection} (PLCP), an efficient closed-form approximation, and the \emph{Parametric Euclidean Conic Projection} (PECP), the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary. Our analysis establishes several fundamental theoretical properties. We prove that PLCP and PECP are collinear, differ only by a positive radial scaling factor, and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold, thereby preserving an identical active support. Furthermore, we derive a support-identification theorem showing that, for any prescribed sparsity level $l<n$, the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is theoretically controlled. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a bilevel PLCP framework for structured matrix sparsification. The proposed method naturally generates hardware-friendly structured sparsity patterns, including row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal masks, making it particularly well suited for accelerating Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Michel Barlaud, Clement Genninasca, Maxime Zanella, Benoit Macq, Benoit Legat
bullets: Defines the scale-invariant Cone Alignment Index (CAI) and analyzes its distribution under general, Gaussian, and uniform settings.
Proposes PLCP, a closed-form conic projection approximation, alongside PECP, the exact Euclidean projection.
Proves PLCP and PECP are collinear, preserve the same sparsity threshold, and identify identical active supports.
Establishes theoretical control over the number of coefficients discarded for a target sparsity level.
Extends PLCP to bilevel matrix sparsification with row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal structured masks.

papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
authors: Sosuke Kobayashi, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Builds a prompt-specific index by clustering noncontiguous keys into large semantic blocks.
Each query scores block centroids, then attends to the original keys and values within selected blocks.
Groups queries selecting the same blocks to keep prefill efficient despite query-specific routing.
On one H200, whole-model speedups reach 2.3–2.4× for 512K prefill, 1.7–2.0× for 512K decoding, and 2.9–3.0× for 1M prefill.
The 35B-A3B model remains close to dense attention on several long-context evaluations; the 4B model mainly degrades on multi-key retrieval.

papers.abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Sahar Dastani, Fereshteh Shakeri, Samuel Barbeau, Kunal Mahatha, Ismail Ben Ayed, Herve Lombaert, Christian Desrosiers
bullets: Addresses the quadratic sequence-length cost of standard self-attention and the limited expressivity of first-order linear attention.
Uses truncated random walks to enable higher-order token interactions within a linear-attention framework.
Employs adaptive locality to emphasize semantically similar neighbors and preserve fine-grained visual structure.
Evaluated on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, with improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
The abstract does not specify numerical gains or experimental datasets.

Aggregating the truncated terms on S yields a global attention map that captures transitive (higher-order) dependencies. In parallel, we compute content-based similarity within each token’s local neighborhood to form a local attention map. The layer output is a convex combination of the two, blending sharp local context with long-range structure.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
bullets: DSA’s full-cache indexer scan dominates decode time at long contexts, while adjacent layers choose nearly identical tokens.
MLI lets each layer attend to the preceding layer’s selection, allowing indexer computation to overlap with attention.
It requires no retraining or new weights; the default implementation runs in SGLang without kernel changes, with an optional fused kernel.
Combined with IndexCache, MLI improves decoding speed by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at equal retention.
Long-context accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and LongBench v2 remains within a few percentage points of IndexCache.
