papers.selection_reason: Optimizes sparse attention and long-context LLM decode, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context model developments.
papers.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) hides DeepSeek Sparse Attention’s expensive indexer scans by reusing the previous layer’s token selection, delivering faster long-context decoding without retraining.

papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
authors: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
bullets: The study tests small language models trained from scratch on web text, code, and mathematics.
It replaces standard transformer activations with learned splines tuned to specific datasets.
Cross-domain evaluations show that architectures tuned for natural language transfer better within language domains, while math-tuned variants perform poorly on natural language.
Improvements appear across all seven tested datasets, with mechanisms linked to wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
The findings suggest domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency while supporting general-purpose models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Validation performance of models trained on three datasets representative of natural language, code, and mathematics. Dots represent models trained with different seeds or nonlinearities (see legend on the left). Coloured outlines represent approximate distributions. The architectures specialized for each target dataset (D1=D2 ) almost always improve over the baselines, whereas the transfer across domains (D1 ̸=D2) varies a lot. We then reuse these frozen components to train a model on a target dataset D2 (right). Only very few parameters are transferred.

Figure 2: Typical training curves during the warmup phase (on CSN-PYTHON here), where we optimize both the weights of transformers and their nonlinearities, initialized as constant functions (left). Figure 7: Baseline models often improve late in training ( ) when the LR reaches tiny values (on FINEWEB, see Figure 14 for other datasets). Figure 14: More examples like Figure 7. The baseline with standard LR decay (--) often improves late during training when the LR reaches very small values. In comparison, our model converges more easily both with (–) and without (–) LR decay.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that domain-specific inductive biases (e.g., learned splines) improve LLM training efficiency and generalization, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
papers.tldr: Domain-specific transformer inductive biases can improve language-model training efficiency or generalization, but their benefits often do not transfer across domains.

papers.abstract: Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes. We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations. Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of $1.10$--$1.40\times$ on B200 and $1.06$--$1.42\times$ on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload. We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.
bullets: Targets attention’s high computational cost at long context lengths on Blackwell GPUs.
Introduces MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 attention kernels with reusable token-block scaling and leakage safeguards.
Maintains consistent forward and backward computations while fusing quantization and applying architecture-specific optimizations.
Supports variable-length causal documents in packed layouts through document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling.
Achieves 1.10–1.40× speedups on B200 and 1.06–1.42× on B300 for the MXFP8 path, while preserving training stability and quality in Llama-style pretraining.

papers.title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reading growing KV histories during long-context inference.
Indexes fixed-size KV chunks using compact key summaries, with one query per KV group and shared selections across group queries.
QShare reuses chunk selections across adjacent prefill queries to reduce indexing overhead and improve KV reuse.
Reports up to 8–16× fewer KV reads, 2.29× end-to-end throughput, and quality within roughly 1.5–2.05 percentage points of dense attention in evaluated settings.
Using fewer chunks raises throughput to 2.61× but widens the GraphWalks quality gap to 3.59 percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: Chunk-indexed sparse attention retrofits dense models, reducing KV reads for long-context inference.
papers.title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: CISA retrofits pretrained dense-attention LLMs with chunk-level sparse attention, achieving substantially faster million-token inference while keeping quality close to dense attention without retraining.

papers.abstract: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.
bullets: Exhaustively scoring every prefix key makes sparse-attention selection a major prefill bottleneck at long contexts.
It routes queries through a causal inverted-file index, then reranks retrieved candidates with the native indexer score.
The index is built online during prefill, immediately includes new keys, reuses prior clustering, and restricts queries to prefix-derived clusters.
On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, it achieves 1.3–1.8× exhaustive-selection prefill throughput.
At similar throughput to HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 more percentage points of exhaustive top-k recall and improves long-context accuracy by up to 18.4 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AttentionIndex for one indexed layer. Update path: new keys enter an open window and are searchable at once; every W keys the window is sealed into local clusters, and every R tokens a refit regroups the prefix. A new index version is visible only to queries whose prefix contains all of its keys.

papers.abstract: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective. We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.
bullets: Targets redundant auxiliary adjoints in chunkwise Delta-rule linear-attention backward passes.
Uses a triangular residual-system formulation plus centered contractions and scalar-gate reductions to expose reuse.
Applies across DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 without changing the architecture or training objective.
Reports 1.15–1.81× geometric-mean low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs and 1.09–2.89× on Ascend 950DT under matched policies.
Validation includes precision-qualified operator checks, ablations, complete-gradient checks, and selected full-model integration measurements.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an algebraic reformulation that reduces backward-pass matrix multiplications for delta-rule linear attention, directly improving attention efficiency.
papers.title: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications
papers.tldr: ReWY reformulates Delta-rule attention backpropagation to reduce seven local WY matrix multiplications to three, delivering faster GPU and NPU backward execution while preserving exact gradients.

papers.abstract: Attention kernels on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) often underutilize their matrix units (MXUs) because of repeated matrix operand loads, vector-intensive computation, and dependencies that leave MXUs idle. We present FlyWheel, a set of fast TPU kernels for both softmax and linear attention. FlyWheel reformulates softmax and triangular inversion to reduce vector work, while coordinating data layouts to improve matrix operand reuse. It then overlaps independent computation to hide execution latency. We apply these techniques to both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x. FlyWheel speeds up softmax attention by up to $4.14\times$ over the state-of-the-art RPA kernel and $1.80\times$ over Splash Attention, reaching 81% of peak BF16 throughput on v6e. It also speeds up Gated DeltaNet prefill by up to $3.61\times$. Integrated into vLLM serving Qwen3.8-27B, FlyWheel improves prefill throughput by up to $1.56\times$ while maintaining comparable accuracy.
bullets: Targets TPU attention kernels whose MXUs are underutilized due to repeated loads, vector-heavy work, and execution dependencies.
Reformulates softmax and triangular inversion, coordinates data layouts for operand reuse, and overlaps independent operations.
Supports both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x.
Achieves up to 4.14× speedup for softmax attention, 3.61× for Gated DeltaNet prefill, and 1.56× higher vLLM prefill throughput while maintaining comparable accuracy.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.
bullets: Diffusion LLMs repeatedly recompute bidirectional attention, causing quadratic cost at every denoising step.
Attention patterns are only locally stable across steps and vary substantially in concentration between heads.
The method refreshes sparse masks at anchor steps and reuses them within locally consistent intervals.
A head-adaptive sparsity budget compresses concentrated heads more aggressively than uniform allocation.
With a fused Triton kernel, it achieves 2.78× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context, 256 steps, and 90% sparsity.

The next ∆−1 steps reuse only these masks, recomputing Q,K, V and the attention weights from the current hidden states (Stage 3). A single query block per head is illustrated.

papers.title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
papers.tldr: Step-dLLM accelerates diffusion LLM inference by adapting block-sparse attention masks to denoising-step changes and attention differences across heads.

papers.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.
bullets: Addresses the pairwise offset computation and memory overhead that hinder efficient relative-position attention.
Introduces offset-aware tiled computation, reusable query/key relation products, and offset-based gradient aggregation without atomic contention.
Provides a unified Triton implementation supporting diverse relative-position attention mechanisms.
At 8K tokens, reports 1.8–6.4× faster forward passes, 2.0–21× faster backward passes, and up to 2.9–128× lower peak memory than the strongest mechanism-specific baselines.
Enables end-to-end long-context transcription that is 1.8× faster and uses 2.4× less memory.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.
bullets: Targets KV-cache capacity limits and decode-attention throughput in long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads.
Uses training-free NVFP4 cache storage, native FP4 query-key computation, dense history scoring, and sparse FP16 value aggregation.
At 128 selected blocks per KV head, no accuracy loss was detected across evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks.
At 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieved a 1.94× end-to-end decode speedup at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300.
Measured Qwen KV pools stored 2.58–2.76× as many tokens as BF16; smaller budgets could reduce accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Presents Jet-QSparse, a training-free method for accelerating LLM inference using 4-bit sparse attention and quantized KV cache, directly relevant to efficient attention and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Jet-QSparse accelerates long-context agentic LLM decoding by combining 4-bit KV-cache storage with sparse attention while preserving evaluated accuracy at a sufficient sparsity budget.

papers.abstract: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. Controlled TPU adaptations of prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations. Preliminary causal LLM experiments also show up to 13.5% higher training throughput in continued pretraining and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling that bottleneck online softmax in long-token TPU attention.
Uses a training-free, plug-and-play optimization that fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies safety per head.
Falls back to online softmax when certification fails, preserving numerical safety while integrating with existing fused-attention kernels.
Evaluated on Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x; preliminary causal LLM tests also report throughput gains.
Scope includes TPU inference and preliminary training results; benefits depend on successful stabilization certification.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free attention stabilization method for video diffusion on TPUs, improving attention efficiency.
papers.title: CLiS: Plug-and-Play Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion on TPUs via Certified Stabilization
papers.tldr: CLiS accelerates long-context video diffusion attention on TPUs by safely fixing softmax stabilizers, reducing DiT step latency by up to 19.6% without measurable quality loss.

papers.abstract: Smartphone applications increasingly require large language models to process long contexts, whereas high prefill latency and memory demands constrain local inference. Block-sparse attention reduces computation and memory traffic, but its irregular selections conflict with mobile NPUs' preference for large, regular tiles. Efficient execution must exploit cross-query reuse while avoiding redundant computation and preserving selections needed for accuracy. In this paper, we present TileWeave, which partitions sparse attention by this cross-query reuse: highly shared key blocks run in coarse NPU tiles, while low-reuse blocks run on the GPU only for the query blocks that selected them. In addition, we design an NPU-native pooled-key selector that keeps selection inexpensive, and a runtime that publishes GPU partials in the order the NPU consumes them and merges them in its existing output store. On RULER, HeteroSparse matches XAttention's accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B and improves it with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; its mean LongBench scores match XAttention as well. On Snapdragon SM8750 and SM8850 phones, it achieves 1.35--3.23$\times$ faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k--16k tokens and up to 1.58$\times$ faster than dense attention.
bullets: Targets long-context mobile inference bottlenecks: high prefill latency and memory demands.
Uses coarse NPU tiles for highly reused key blocks and GPU execution for low-reuse blocks selected by specific query blocks.
Adds an NPU-native pooled-key selector and runtime coordination for ordered GPU partials and NPU-side merging.
Matches XAttention accuracy on Qwen3-1.7B and mean LongBench scores, while improving accuracy on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.
On Snapdragon SM8750/SM8850, delivers 1.35–3.23× faster full-model prefill than XAttention and up to 1.58× faster than dense attention across 1k–16k tokens.

papers.title: TileWeave: Heterogeneous Tiling for Sparse Prefill on Mobile SoCs
papers.tldr: TileWeave accelerates sparse LLM prefill on mobile SoCs by assigning attention work to NPUs or GPUs based on cross-query reuse while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant, Benjamin Hoover, Fraser Greenlee, Ruairidh M. Battleday, Radim Urban, Torsten Hoefler, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Targets the prohibitive cost and accuracy degradation of existing sparse attention beyond 1M tokens.
Organizes keys into a learned latent hierarchy, allowing queries to score clusters rather than all keys.
Introduces Distilled-LSA for adapting pretrained models and Native-LSA for native next-token-loss training.
At 10M tokens, D-LSA substantially accelerates prefill and decode while maintaining similar accuracy across evaluated tasks.
N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy and provides per-layer training speedups at 128k tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Subquadratic sparse attention for ultra-long context via latent hierarchical key selection; directly fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.tldr: Latent Sparse Attention enables efficient ultra-long-context attention by hierarchically routing queries to learned key clusters instead of examining every key.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Figure 8: For a fixed top-p, and hence sparsity level, ZHA (here, R = 1, C = 8, p = 0.75) scales subquadratically according to our decode roofline model, eventually dramatically outperforming both dense attention and the MSA sparse attention variant. Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

papers.title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
papers.tldr: Zyphra Hierarchical Attention uses a recursively compressed tree index to achieve subquadratic sparse attention for very long-context LLMs while preserving key task performance.

papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
authors: Zhangchi Feng, Harry Jiang, Yangyifei Luo, Ray Zhang, Richong Zhang
bullets: Finite-state memory and initialization can limit long-context retrieval in linear attention.
DAMI jointly configures gate parameters before training using geometric head-wise timescales and a low-high-low layer-wise sensitivity profile.
A small activation sample calibrates the implementation to these targets without adding trainable parameters.
Across five gated linear-attention families, DAMI raises average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29–16.71 percentage points over random initialization.
Language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval performance remains broadly comparable to baseline initialization.

papers.abstract: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.
bullets: Addresses Transformer KV-cache growth and the limited addressability of fixed-state State Space Models.
Uses multiple complex-diagonal dynamical memory units with input-dependent leak rates to encode sequences.
A decoder attends to memory outputs rather than the full token history; recurrence supports O(T) work and O(log T) parallel depth.
Matches Transformer closely in language modeling, outperforms both baselines on several cognitive tasks, and remains behind Mamba on language modeling.
Shows stronger selective-copy length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer; performance has task-dependent limitations.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
authors: Cheng Liang, Tengfei Zhang, Ya Zhang, Yanfeng Wang, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped models can improve reasoning through shared-weight repeated computation, but normally require more training FLOPs.
UpLoop starts with a shallow Transformer, copies learned layers to grow depth, and later repeats a shared middle block.
It exactly matches a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, training tokens, and total training FLOPs.
Across model scales, it improves language modeling and downstream performance; at 1.3B parameters, the 22-task average rises from 22.99 to 27.52.
Benefits also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.
authors: Ziteng Wang, Jianqiao Lu, Xinyu Ma, Jintao Zhang, Jun Zhu, Yiyuan Ma, Jianfei Chen
bullets: Problem: Standard residuals force the state width carried through depth to match each layer’s compute width.
Method: Group layers into blocks with d-dimensional PreNorm layers and a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual, linked by learned projections.
Contribution: Makes residual width an independent scaling variable using only dense projections and normalizations.
Results: Reports 1.30× better FLOPs efficiency, 0.0208 lower training loss, and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy in the stated experiments.
Scope: Designed to reduce activation memory and I/O relative to other residual-expansion methods without specialized kernels or infrastructure changes.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), an architectural efficiency improvement for Transformers that decouples residual width from compute width.
papers.title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width
papers.tldr: HiRes decouples residual width from per-layer compute width, improving scaling efficiency with a simple Transformer modification.

papers.abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.
authors: Wenbo Fu, Chenghui Mao, Chengwen Hu, Haifeng Lv, Zhou Lv
bullets: Addresses the tension between local neighbor graphs that miss long-range interactions and quadratic-cost all-pair attention.
Maps centroid-relative atomic distances to learned radial features and combines them with content-dependent queries and keys.
Uses factorized aggregation and readout for linear scaling with atom count at fixed feature dimensions.
Inserted between EquiformerV3 local blocks, with conservative forces obtained by differentiating the energy.
On OPoly26 polymer-derived clusters, matched 5M models reduce per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%; the 20M model achieves 15.81 meV total-energy MAE and 2.619 meV/angstrom force MAE.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RKA in an equivariant atomic potential. Each local block updates the geometric representation. RKA reads its scalar channels and positions, and writes a scalar residual before the next block. The final scalar readout gives atomic energies. Shared elemental references and screened repulsion complete the total energy, whose coordinate derivative defines the forces. Charge/spin conditioning and repulsion are present in both 5M models.

Figure 1: Radial Kernel Attention. A finite structure defines a centroid and node radii. Learned radial features organize content-dependent key–value statistics over the entire structure. Each node reads the shared statistics through its radial features and query, and receives a scalar residual update. The basis curves are schematic, rather than fitted checkpoint values.
Table 1: Configurations of our polymer force fields. The 5M pair shares its local architecture, conditioning, and repulsion. Parameter counts are reported in millions to two decimal places.

Table 3: Complete-model comparison on all 201,865 official validation structures, with no skipped structures. Parameter counts are the reported model totals in millions. All error columns are MAEs; lower is better.

Table 2: Effect of RKA on the shared 5M backbone. Both models include charge/spin conditioning and screened repulsion, train for 12 epochs, and use the same official validation structures. Lower MAE is better.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in force fields, achieving linear complexity in atom count through factorized aggregation.
papers.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
papers.tldr: Radial Kernel Attention adds a linear-cost global communication pathway that substantially improves energy and force prediction for polymer machine-learning force fields.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.tldr: A dual-budget framework analyzes sparse diffusion models by separately constraining attention connectivity and expert activation, with reported gains through 16K tokens but degradation at longer lengths and a 20% cost reduction under an unspecified timing convention.

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3 End-to-end SparseGDN execution pipeline. The block-adjacent intra-chunk kernel computes transformed values U, compact update coefficients, and selector scores. The dynamic selector converts these scores into a structured event mask. Only selected events trigger deferred W materialization and recurrent-state updates, producing compact event states. During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

papers.title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention

papers.abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of attention with increasing context length by compressing the KV cache.
Formulates attention in a kernel-associated Hilbert space, representing it as a ratio of linear maps whose interpolants can be compressed directly.
Proposes GAIM and Q-DAIM methods based on GEIM and Q-DEIM interpolation techniques.
Uses Taylor-series, Performer, and Random Fourier Features surrogates to reduce compression cost from quadratic to linear time, and extends the approach to streaming attention.

Numerical experiments evaluate residual and future-query output errors; preliminary LongBench-E results show performance comparable to existing methods, while suggesting Q-DAIM can reveal where KV-cache information is concentrated.

papers.abstract: We present FloodDiffusion 2 (FD2), an efficient and controllable framework that builds upon FloodDiffusion (FD1), a state-of-the-art streaming motion generation model. While FD1 produces plausible motion, it suffers from low efficiency and limited controllability, as its attention design requires repeated computation over the entire history, and it lacks precise trajectory control for real-world applications. To address these limitations and improve generation quality, FD2 introduces three advances. First, Partial Attention makes finalized history representations independent of the active window, enabling KV-cached inference and shared-history packing for efficient training. Second, we establish a necessary-and-sufficient Bregman criterion for regression losses to preserve diffusion's conditional-mean velocity field. This criterion guides an FK-induced quadratic loss that incorporates motion geometry without online FK evaluation. Third, FD2 introduces precise path conditioning to control the character's root trajectory while preserving natural body motion. Experiments show that FD2 reduces training computation by 4.6$\times$ and accelerates denoising by 11.29$\times$, reaching 2.303 ms per update on long sequences. Alongside these efficiency gains, FD2 improves motion quality over FD1 and achieves state-of-the-art FID scores among streaming methods, with 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.
bullets: Targets FD1’s repeated-history computation and limited trajectory control.
Uses Partial Attention for KV-cached inference and shared-history packing during training.
Introduces a Bregman-based criterion and FK-induced quadratic loss to incorporate motion geometry without online forward-kinematics evaluation.
Adds precise root-path conditioning while preserving natural full-body motion.
Reports 4.6× lower training computation, 11.29× faster denoising, and improved FID over FD1, including 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.
bullets: Extends Single Location Regression to 2D structured data for analyzing sparse-information settings.
Introduces an analytically tractable axial-attention predictor and studies its statistical properties and training dynamics.
Proves Bayes optimality in a specific asymptotic regime when oracle parameters are known.
Shows semi-linear simplifications fail strictly, emphasizing the importance of the inner non-linearity.
Proves global convergence of Projected Gradient Descent under a specific temperature scaling; experiments support the theory and the role of inverse-temperature scheduling.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in gigapixel-level imaging have brought High-Resolution Wide shots to the forefront of research. However, these images present significant challenges: extreme sparsity of foreground, gigapixel-level resolutions and diverse target counts. This makes traditional close-up detectors inaccurate and slow as they are overwhelmed by the background. Although previous research has explored sparse backbones, their fixed sparsity patterns lack the adaptability required to handle diverse target numbers. To address this, we introduce ElasticFormer, a sparse backbone that dynamically allocates computational resources based on foreground proportion. After scoring windows based on variance, proposed ElasticSelector module will predict the foreground proportion for top-k selection. The mechanism guides the model to select target-containing windows, scaling resources in areas where objects are clustered. We introduce a novel loss function combined with the 3-phase training strategy for ElasticSelector, allowing it to function properly when bounding box annotations are missing. A WSOD study is carried on PASCAL VOC 2007 to evaluate its extensibility. Further, ElasticNet is created to verify its backbone-agnostic nature. In experiments on the PANDA gigapixel benchmark, ElasticFormer reduces backbone FLOPs by 80% while achieving a significant improvement in AP50 when compared to fixed-ratio sparse methods.
authors: Wenxi Li, Jingchen Huang, Chenyang Lyu, Moran Liu, Haozhe Lin, Guiguang Ding, Yuchen Guo
bullets: Targets sparse, extremely high-resolution images with few objects and variable target counts, where conventional detectors are slow and inaccurate.
Scores image windows by variance, then uses ElasticSelector to estimate foreground proportions and choose top-k regions adaptively.

On PANDA, reduces backbone FLOPs by 80% and significantly improves AP50 over fixed-ratio sparse methods.
Evaluates extensibility on PASCAL VOC 2007 WSOD and develops ElasticNet to demonstrate backbone compatibility.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in gigapixel-level imaging have brought High-Resolution Wide shots to the forefront of research. However, these images present significant challenges: extreme sparsity of foreground, gigapixel-level resolutions and interleaving of foreground and background. This causes traditional detectors and attention mechanisms to be hindered by background, resulting in inefficiency and inaccuracy. To tackle this problem, we propose BiHashFormer, a dual sparsified branch transformer built on hashing. RoI Selector will predict the foreground proportion for top-k selecting target-containing windows. The compression branch processes windows selected and refines attention into HashAttention by discarding half of the key-value pairs, reducing cost and improving efficiency. The compensation branch uses HashMiner to perform low-cost hash searches in the remaining regions, recovering features of missed objects. Experiments confirm that the selection relationship in HashAttention is one-way and reveal the preference of different queries for keys. In experiments on the gigapixel benchmark PANDA, BiHashFormer reduces 37.5% backbone FLOPs while improving AP50 to 81.0%. Moreover, this parallel dual-branch structure allows the model to avoid inference delays caused by inter-branch dependencies, while achieving much greater stability than single-branch models, specially with low rates of RoI selection.
authors: Jingchen Huang, Wenxi Li, Chenyang Lyu, Moran Liu, Haozhe Lin, Yuchen Guo
bullets: Targets sparse foreground by selecting the top-k windows most likely to contain objects.

A compensation branch uses low-cost HashMiner searches in unselected regions to recover missed objects.
On PANDA, it reduces backbone FLOPs by 37.5% and reaches 81.0% AP50.
Parallel branches avoid inter-branch inference delays and remain more stable at low RoI-selection rates.

papers.tldr: BiHashFormer uses hash-based dual-branch attention to efficiently detect objects in sparse, gigapixel wide-shot images while recovering missed targets.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but the quadratic cost of 3D full attention dominates their inference. Dynamic block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing exact attention only on key/value blocks selected from current activations. However, its fidelity degrades under aggressive sparsity: blocks are scored from coarse summaries or formed by costly global clustering, pruned blocks vanish from the softmax, and whole tiles are kept or dropped even when only a few of their keys matter. To address these limitations, we propose Accurate Block Attention (AB-Attention), a training-free method that accurately approximates dense attention at high sparsity. Its Intra-Block Clustering Selector (IBCS) estimates block importance faithfully yet cheaply by clustering queries only within each query block, without permuting tokens. Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting (SIP) then samples blocks in proportion to these estimates and reweights them by inverse inclusion probability, so that one pass estimates dense attention rather than truncating it. Finally, its kernel gathers key/value blocks much smaller than a tile into full tensor-core tiles, refining selection at no extra tensor-core cost. On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, AB-Attention skips 89--92\% of attention, whereas the baselines compute 1.8--3.6$\times$ as much, yet it still improves PSNR by up to 4.4~dB over the strongest baseline and achieves up to 2.23$\times$ end-to-end speedup. Our code is available at https://github.com/InfRec-Cardinal/AB-Attention.
authors: Bin Xu, Mo Zhang, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Xinfeng Yang, Yixing Ma, Wei Wang, HeXin Wang, Pengfei Zhou, Wangbo Zhao
bullets: Targets the quadratic inference cost of 3D full attention and fidelity loss under aggressive block sparsity.
Uses Intra-Block Clustering Selector (IBCS) to estimate block importance from queries within each query block.
Applies Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting (SIP) to estimate dense attention instead of simply dropping unselected blocks.
Gathers smaller key/value blocks into tensor-core tiles for finer-grained selection without extra tensor-core cost.
On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, skips 89–92% of attention, improves PSNR by up to 4.4 dB over the strongest baseline, and reaches up to 2.23× end-to-end speedup.

papers.abstract: Unlimited OCR ushers the era of long-horizon parsing, substantially mitigating the growth of working memory as document lengthens. However, as document length scales to hundreds of pages, the visual context grows substantially, sharply increasing the computational cost of each decoding step and limiting the scalability of ultra-long document parsing. Inspired by human book transcription via localized focus without re-scanning preceding pages, we introduce Unlimited OCR 2, a document parsing model that looks only at what it transcribes. Building on Unlimited OCR, we upgrade all the decoder attention modules to Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), bounding active reference tokens to a fixed capacity and thus sustaining constant computational costs across arbitrarily long documents. By combining SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm, Unlimited OCR 2 enables document parsing over virtually unlimited lengths without prohibitive memory overhead. At the hundred-page scale, Unlimited OCR 2 achieves 7.0$\times$ and 5.6$\times$ per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA, respectively. Furthermore, it delivers state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on both MPDocBench and MarathonDocBench, our newly proposed benchmark targeting hundred-page document parsing. Ultimately, the capacity for uninterrupted, one-shot document parsing signifies a fundamental paradigm shift into the OCR 3.0 era.
authors: Shu Wei, Jingjing Wu, Qunyi Xie, Lingshu Zhang, Xiangcheng Du, Yannian Fu, Mengjie Wang, Zuyi Wang, Zhichao Liu, Yangliu Xu, YY, Yi Yang
bullets: Addresses the rising per-step computation and memory costs of parsing documents hundreds of pages long.
Introduces Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), which bounds active reference tokens to a fixed capacity.
Combines SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding for constant-cost decoding across document lengths.
At the hundred-page scale, reports 7.0× and 5.6× per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA.
Achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end results on MPDocBench and the proposed MarathonDocBench.

figures.caption: Figure 5 | Performance comparison on multi-page benchmarks. Unlimited OCR 2 (Ours) consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation categories.

Figure 3 | Inspired by the process of humans copying books, we propose Unlimited OCR 2. SRSWA combines Page Gate and Token Sieve to construct a fixed-length set of working reference visual tokens, substantially reducing computational and memory overhead while keeping both independent of document length throughout generation.

Figure 4 | Comparison of (a) standard decoding and (b) our Unlimited-Horizon Decoding paradigm. Standard decoding retains visual KV caches for all pages, causing GPU memory usage to grow linearly with document length and eventually overflow. Our paradigm divides long documents into manageable chunks and processes them sequentially, reusing the KV cache of shared boundary pages and releasing inactive caches to keep GPU memory usage bounded while preserving cross-chunk continuity.

papers.abstract: Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce CACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. CACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.
authors: Kwun Fung Lau, Frost Mitchell, Kanya Mo, Emani Ashok
bullets: Targets CPU attention bottlenecks caused by multi-tier cache hierarchies and inefficient thread scheduling.
Uses tiered cache blocking with in-kernel task dispatch for causal full-sequence prefilling.
Reports up to 2.01× speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels.
Integrated with SGLang, it reduces Llama-3.1-8B TTFT by up to 1.74× while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is not merely long-sequence modeling. Once the volume is packed, sequence order no longer encodes the geometry of the sample---so a positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can learn the memory layout rather than the object. This is a general failure mode for attention over packed geometric data. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and indexes every query-key interaction with axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates rather than packed positions. Because the rotation is applied before a block is summarized, the query-to-summary logit remains a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements; compressed global context therefore stays spatially interpretable after packing, instead of collapsing to anonymous pooled content. We measure the failure mode directly. On a controlled synthetic task---train on one packing, change only the memory order of the tokens, hold the physical labeling rule fixed---learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE solve the training layout perfectly yet collapse under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact throughout. The same coordinate system carries to real data: on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, with controls isolating the coordinate system, not encoder capacity, as the source of the gain. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while supplying the long-range context windowing cannot---so the operator is not only correct but trainable at scale.
authors: Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath
bullets: Packed sequence positions can encode memory layout rather than physical object geometry.
PACK3D combines exact local attention with compressed summaries of distant 3D blocks.
Axial RoPE uses true token-grid coordinates, keeping query-to-summary relationships spatially interpretable.
On a controlled repacking task, packed-position methods fail after reordering, while grid-coordinate RoPE remains exact.
On hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over matched 3D U-Net and learned-position baselines; a fused implementation scales to 65k tokens with windowed-attention latency.

papers.selection_reason: Packed 3D attention with axial coordinate RoPE; core technical contribution is efficient local-global attention over geometrically structured 3D volumes.
papers.title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention
papers.tldr: PACK3D preserves 3D geometry in attention over packed volumes by using true grid coordinates for local and compressed global interactions, remaining robust to token repacking.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. Code: https://github.com/ReichtumQian/DualDeltaNet
authors: Yixiao Qian, Yaxin Zhang, Song Chen, Jiaxu Liu, Shengze Cai, Chao Xu
bullets: Targets interference and poor organization in fixed-size recurrent states used by linear attention and SSMs.
Extends Kimi Delta Attention with complementary key-side and value-side delta rules.
Introduces chunkwise parallel training and a rank-2 recurrence for higher inference arithmetic intensity.
Reports strongest overall performance among DDN, KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3 across language modeling, zero-shot tasks, and retrieval.
Adds modest training and inference overhead compared with KDA.

papers.abstract: Perception tasks for navigation in robotics, including aerial platforms such as drones and autonomous driving systems, are inherently structured. Drone-mounted cameras typically capture sky above, terrain below, and obstacles or man-made structures in between, while driving data often contains organized road layouts, lane markings, and surrounding agents. Motivated by these axis-aligned structural priors, we note that such information is typically more structured than in generic image tasks. We hypothesize that processing information in a quadtree-esque manner can not only model features effectively in a hierarchical manner, but also offers an efficient linear-time alternative to vanilla attention mechanisms, which run in quadratic time. In this paper, we propose Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA), which models image tokens hierarchically as a structured, full quadtree. We show analytical complexity analysis that guarantees linear-time feature modeling, in addition to empirical experiments comparing inference speeds with other popular modeling approaches, such as Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention. Our results, benchmarked across several tasks, show that we achieve results at least as good, if not notably better, as others at a fraction of the computational costs.
authors: Yufan Chen, Arnav Bali, Angela Liu, Laura Zheng, Ming C. Lin
bullets: Targets structured navigation perception in robotics, including drones and autonomous driving.
Organizes image tokens as a structured full quadtree based on axis-aligned scene priors.
Introduces sibling-selective attention to support hierarchical feature modeling.
Provides analytical guarantees of linear-time complexity instead of quadratic vanilla attention.
Experiments across several tasks report competitive or better results at a fraction of the computational cost, including comparisons with Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Mean Epoch Wall Times (s) across 50 epochs on IllusionAnimals classification (2242 inputs) on A100 GPU. Despite other methods also modeling attention in linear time, a practical caveat is the lack of compute optimization in practice. As a result, some methods are even slower than vanilla ViT [6] out-of-the-box from official implementations. SSQA is both easy to integrate and requires no additional practical optimizations, our results show that SSQA maintains or even improves performance over other hierarchical modeling baselines.

Fig. 2: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up Gating; Squares indicate leaf nodes. Our work has a key difference from previous work in hierarchical quadtree-based attention approaches: bottom-up gating. Previous works (a) avoid subdivisions into tokens with smaller granularity if possible by selecting top-k tokens with highest saliency during training. As a result, tokens on the same level outside of top-k saliency neglect hierarchical reasoning, even if there agents present in those patches. For example, in a driving scene, one patch may have a higher density of pedestrians, but it shouldn’t imply less attention on the single agent falling outside of the same patch. In our approach, we model features from bottom-up, ensuring that features are modeled hierarchically across the entire image. Doing so not only improves performance on various benchmarked tasks, but also maintains linear complexity with respect to number of tokens (shown in §III-G).
Fig. 4: Model Efficiency. SSQA is substantially lighter by reducing the number of parameters by nearly 3x and more compute-efficient by up to a factor of 8x for classification test.
Fig. 3: Training Dynamics. SSQA (a) converges faster and (b) reaches target accuracy earlier than the ViT baseline.

papers.abstract: LLM-based generative recommendation reads long, text-rich interaction histories but generates only short semantic identifiers (SIDs). This asymmetry makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient: encoding the history is expensive, yet each history usually provides supervision for only one target. We present Merge and Branch (M&B) to reduce input cost and learn more from each encoded history. Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens. Branch uses the compressed history to predict multiple target SIDs. To share history computation while keeping these targets independent, M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree. We develop tree FlashAttention to execute this layout efficiently, processing the shared history once and propagating gradients from every branch for end-to-end training. A tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding. Experiments on public benchmarks show that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency.
bullets: Addresses the costly encoding of long, text-rich histories when each history typically supervises only one short semantic identifier.
Merge compresses each historical item’s SID and text into a few learned tokens; Branch predicts multiple target SIDs from the shared representation.
Uses a shallow, wide tree with tree FlashAttention to share history computation while keeping target branches independent.
A tree-structured key/value cache extends computation sharing to constrained decoding.
On public benchmarks, it outperforms strong baselines while improving training and decoding efficiency.
